meta.blurb: Matthew Cuthbert goes to the station to fetch an orphan boy and comes home with a red-haired girl who never stops talking. Marilla wants to send her back. Anne has other plans, and plenty of mistakes still to make.
meta.bible: Anne Shirley: an eleven-year-old orphan with red hair, a huge imagination and a quick temper; she spells her name with an e. Matthew Cuthbert: an old, shy, gentle farmer who loves Anne at once. Marilla Cuthbert: his sister, stern, practical and kind underneath. Mrs Rachel Lynde: the nosy, outspoken neighbour. Diana Barry: Anne's best friend, her bosom friend, dark-haired and kind. Mrs Barry: Diana's mother, who is strict. Minnie May: Diana's little sister, who has croup. Gilbert Blythe: a clever, handsome schoolboy who teases Anne about her red hair and later becomes her friend. Mr Phillips: the first teacher at Avonlea school. Miss Stacy: the inspiring new teacher. Josie Pye: a girl at school, spiteful and proud. Mrs Spencer: the woman who brought Anne to Bright River. Mr Allan: the minister at Avonlea. Mrs Allan: his wife, loved by Anne. Mr Barry: Diana's father, who rents Green Gables land. Green Gables: the Cuthberts' farmhouse. Avonlea: the village on Prince Edward Island. Bright River: the railway station. White Way of Delight: Anne's name for the apple-tree road. Lake of Shining Waters: Anne's name for Barry's Pond. Queen's Academy: the teachers' college in Charlottetown. Charlottetown: the island's main town. Redmond: the college Anne could attend. Carmody: a nearby village with a school. Prince Edward Island: Canada. Hopetown: where the orphan asylum was. Author: L. M. Montgomery, 1908. Voice and tone: warm, funny and affectionate, full of nature and imagination; sad moments, including Matthew's death, are stated gently and plainly; the ending is hopeful. Added for the full-length book: Miss Josephine Barry: Diana's rich, sharp-tongued great-aunt in Charlottetown; Aunt Josephine is the name the girls use. Mrs Peter Blewett: a hard, sharp-faced woman who wanted a girl to work for her. Ruby Gillis, Jane Andrews, Charlie Sloane, Moody Spurgeon MacPherson: Anne's classmates; Jane and Ruby are her friends, Josie Pye is not. Dr Spencer: the doctor who comes to Minnie May. Walter and Bertha Shirley: Anne's parents, who died of fever when she was three months old. Mrs Thomas and Mrs Hammond: the women who kept Anne before the asylum; Mrs Hammond had three pairs of twins. Katie Maurice and Violetta: Anne's imaginary friends, a reflection and an echo. Snow Queen: the great cherry tree outside Anne's window. Bonny: Anne's name for the geranium. Dryad's Bubble: the spring in the woods. Violet Vale: the hollow of wild flowers. Lover's Lane: the lane of arching trees where Anne and Diana walk. Haunted Wood: the dark spruce grove near Orchard Slope. Orchard Slope: the Barrys' farm. Lily Maid: Elaine, from Tennyson's poem, whom Anne plays in a boat. Tennyson: the poet. Abbey Bank: the bank that failed, with Matthew's savings. John Blythe: Gilbert's father, with whom Marilla once quarrelled. White Sands Hotel: where Anne recites. Avery scholarship: for the best student in English, four years at Redmond. Queen's Academy: in Charlottetown, where Anne studies for a year. Miss Stacy: Muriel Stacy, the teacher who starts the Queen's class. Scotch roses: the white rose bush Matthew's mother brought; Anne lays them with Matthew. Chapters: twenty, ten beats each; the story follows the novel in order, with the three levels in step.
chapters: More Words Than Matthew Had Heard
Green Hair and a Leaking Boat

beats.scene: Mrs Lynde sits knitting at a window above a brook in the hollow
beats.summary: Mrs Rachel Lynde watches the whole village from her window beside the main road.

beats.scene: Matthew Cuthbert drives past in a buggy, wearing a white collar and best suit
beats.summary: Matthew Cuthbert drives past in his best clothes, which is very strange.

beats.scene: Mrs Lynde walks up the lane to Green Gables through the orchard
beats.summary: After tea, Mrs Lynde walks up to Green Gables to question Marilla.

beats.scene: Marilla sits by the kitchen window explaining her plan to Mrs Lynde
beats.summary: Marilla explains that a boy from a Nova Scotia orphan asylum is coming on the evening train.

beats.scene: Mrs Lynde shakes her head, warning Marilla about orphan boys
beats.summary: Mrs Lynde is shocked and warns Marilla that taking in a stranger is a dangerous risk.

beats.scene: Marilla stands firm, thinking of Matthew's age and his weak heart
beats.summary: Marilla explains that Matthew is growing old and weak and that good farm help is hard to find.

beats.scene: Matthew drives a buggy along a red country road beneath blossoming orchards
beats.summary: Matthew drives eight miles to Bright River in the beautiful evening light.

beats.scene: Matthew in the buggy, anxious, remembering the boy and all the women he fears
beats.summary: Matthew worries about the boy and about how shy he feels with every woman except Marilla.

beats.scene: Matthew reaches the empty Bright River platform, where one small girl sits
beats.summary: At Bright River the train is gone, and the only person waiting is a little girl.

beats.scene: The stationmaster points at the girl while Matthew stares in dismay
beats.summary: The stationmaster says the girl came on the train for Matthew, who is horrified.

beats.scene: Anne jumps up from the shingles and holds out her hand to Matthew
beats.summary: Anne greets Matthew warmly and says she was ready to spend the night in a cherry tree.

beats.scene: A thin freckled girl with red braids holds an old carpet bag
beats.summary: Matthew sees a thin, freckled girl in a short faded dress, with two long braids of red hair.

beats.scene: Matthew helps Anne into the buggy and the mare trots away
beats.summary: They drive away from the station, and Anne begins to talk about everything she sees.

beats.scene: A long tunnel of white apple blossoms arches over the road
beats.summary: Anne names the arch of apple blossoms the White Way of Delight.

beats.scene: A shining pond lies at the foot of a hill at sunset
beats.summary: Anne renames Barry's Pond the Lake of Shining Waters.

beats.scene: Anne points at the red road and asks questions, her eyes bright
beats.summary: Anne asks why the roads on the island are red, and Matthew does not know.

beats.scene: Anne talks about never having belonged to anyone, and hopes for a friend
beats.summary: Anne says she has never belonged to anyone, and she hopes to find a bosom friend.

beats.scene: Matthew listens to Anne chatter, and finds that he does not mind
beats.summary: Matthew discovers that he likes listening to Anne, although he is not used to it.

beats.scene: A lamplit farmhouse stands among dark trees as Marilla opens the door
beats.summary: At Green Gables, Marilla opens the door and stares at the girl in the buggy.

beats.scene: Anne sobs with her hands to her face in the kitchen doorway
beats.summary: Anne understands that nobody wanted a girl and bursts into tears.

beats.scene: Marilla and Matthew stand puzzled while Anne cries at the kitchen table
beats.summary: Marilla and Matthew puzzle over the mistake while Anne weeps.

beats.scene: Anne sits before bread, butter and preserves she cannot eat
beats.summary: Anne is too sad to eat, and she asks Marilla to call her Cordelia.

beats.scene: Marilla leads Anne with a candle to a bare white room under the roof
beats.summary: Marilla takes Anne to the east gable room, and Anne cries herself to sleep.

beats.scene: Matthew and Marilla talk quietly in the lamplit kitchen at night
beats.summary: Marilla says Mrs Spencer must take the girl back, but Matthew says she is a nice little thing.

beats.scene: Anne at the east window sees a huge cherry tree covered with blossom
beats.summary: Anne wakes to sunshine and a cherry tree in bloom outside her window.

beats.scene: Anne sits at the breakfast table, too unhappy to eat
beats.summary: Anne says she is in the depths of despair and cannot eat any breakfast.

beats.scene: Anne tells her story across the table while Marilla listens
beats.summary: Anne tells Marilla that her parents, teachers from Bolingbroke, died of fever when she was a baby.

beats.scene: Anne describes working for Mrs Thomas and Mrs Hammond, with crowds of children
beats.summary: Anne tells how she looked after Mrs Thomas's children and then Mrs Hammond's twins.

beats.scene: Anne tells of her imaginary friends in a bookcase glass and a woodland echo
beats.summary: Anne describes her lonely time at the asylum and her imaginary friends Katie Maurice and Violetta.

beats.scene: Matthew leans on the barn door speaking to Marilla in the yard
beats.summary: Matthew tells Marilla that he would like to keep Anne.

beats.scene: Marilla and Anne ride together in the buggy along a sunny country road
beats.summary: Marilla drives Anne to White Sands to see Mrs Spencer, and Anne decides to enjoy the drive.

beats.scene: Mrs Spencer throws up her hands in a farmhouse porch
beats.summary: Mrs Spencer is dismayed to learn that the Cuthberts wanted a boy, and says a message must have been muddled.

beats.scene: A sharp-faced woman looks Anne over with a cold eye
beats.summary: Mrs Peter Blewett, who wants a girl, arrives and inspects Anne.

beats.scene: Marilla draws herself up and decides to take Anne home
beats.summary: Marilla decides that she will not give the child to Mrs Blewett and takes Anne back to Green Gables.

beats.scene: Anne rides home in the buggy and listens to Marilla's decision
beats.summary: On the way home Marilla tells Anne that she may stay if she tries to be good.

beats.scene: Anne kneels by her bed with Marilla standing at the door
beats.summary: Anne has never learned to say her prayers, because Mrs Thomas told her God made her hair red on purpose.

beats.scene: Anne prays in her own way beside the east gable window
beats.summary: Anne makes up a prayer thanking God for the White Way of Delight, the Lake of Shining Waters and the Snow Queen.

beats.scene: Marilla gives Anne a prayer to learn from a small book
beats.summary: Marilla tells Anne to learn a proper prayer and begins to plan her upbringing.

beats.scene: Anne sits sewing patchwork squares at the kitchen table and sighs
beats.summary: Marilla sets Anne to sew patchwork, which Anne dislikes because it leaves no room for imagination.

beats.scene: Mrs Lynde climbs the lane to Green Gables in the afternoon sun
beats.summary: Mrs Lynde, who has been ill for two weeks, comes to see the child.

beats.scene: Mrs Lynde looks Anne up and down in the Green Gables kitchen
beats.summary: Mrs Lynde looks Anne over and says the Cuthberts did not choose her for her looks.

beats.scene: Mrs Lynde points at Anne's freckles and hair
beats.summary: Mrs Lynde calls Anne skinny and plain, and says her hair is as red as carrots.

beats.scene: Anne stamps her foot and shouts at Mrs Lynde
beats.summary: Anne loses her temper, stamps her foot and tells Mrs Lynde that she hates her.

beats.scene: Marilla sends Anne upstairs while Mrs Lynde gathers her shawl
beats.summary: Marilla sends Anne to her room, and Mrs Lynde warns that she will have her hands full.

beats.scene: Anne lies on her bed, refusing to come down or eat
beats.summary: Anne stays in her room, and Marilla says she will not eat until she apologises.

beats.scene: Matthew creeps upstairs to Anne's door and speaks quietly
beats.summary: Matthew tiptoes up to Anne's room and tells her it would be wise to apologise.

beats.scene: Anne kneels dramatically before Mrs Lynde in her kitchen
beats.summary: Anne kneels before Mrs Lynde and makes a grand and tearful apology.

beats.scene: Mrs Lynde laughs kindly and tells Anne her hair may darken
beats.summary: Mrs Lynde forgives Anne and says that her red hair may turn a handsome auburn when she is older.

beats.scene: Anne walks to church in a hat covered with buttercups and wild roses
beats.summary: On Sunday Anne trims her hat with buttercups and wild roses and walks to church feeling splendid.

beats.scene: Anne sits in the church pew while neighbours stare at her flowery hat
beats.summary: At church the neighbours stare at Anne's hat, but she enjoys the singing and the service.

beats.scene: Marilla frowns at the flower-covered hat on the kitchen table
beats.summary: Marilla scolds Anne about the hat of wild flowers, and Anne promises to wear plain ones.

beats.scene: Anne walks through a green wood with a basket on her arm
beats.summary: Marilla sends Anne on an errand to Orchard Slope, and Anne walks there nervously.

beats.scene: Two girls meet beside a garden fence among willows and roses
beats.summary: Anne meets Diana Barry, a dark-haired, rosy-cheeked girl, in the garden at Orchard Slope.

beats.scene: Anne asks Diana to be her bosom friend, with her hands clasped
beats.summary: Anne asks Diana whether she could like her enough to be her bosom friend.

beats.scene: Anne and Diana join hands and swear an oath of friendship in the garden
beats.summary: Anne and Diana swear a solemn oath to be faithful friends for as long as the sun and moon shall endure.

beats.scene: Anne skips home through the wood, her face glowing
beats.summary: Anne returns to Green Gables full of joy and tells Marilla that she has found a bosom friend.

beats.scene: Anne names a hollow of violets and a spring in the woods
beats.summary: Anne and Diana play in the woods and give names to their favourite places, such as the Dryad's Bubble and Violet Vale.

beats.scene: Anne dreams about the Sunday school picnic with her chin in her hands
beats.summary: Marilla tells Anne that the Sunday school picnic is on Wednesday, and Anne can think of nothing else.

beats.scene: Marilla stands before an empty pincushion on her dressing table
beats.summary: On Monday evening Marilla's amethyst brooch is missing from her pincushion.

beats.scene: Marilla questions Anne sternly in the kitchen by the lamp
beats.summary: Anne admits that she tried on the brooch and put it back, but Marilla does not believe her.

beats.scene: Anne in her room tells Marilla a grand made-up confession
beats.summary: To be allowed to go to the picnic, Anne makes up a story that she took the brooch and lost it in the pond.

beats.scene: Marilla sits grimly at the kitchen table, shocked and angry
beats.summary: Marilla is shocked by the confession and forbids Anne to go to the picnic.

beats.scene: Marilla finds her brooch caught in the fringe of her shawl
beats.summary: On the morning of the picnic Marilla finds the brooch hanging in the fringe of her black shawl.

beats.scene: Marilla speaks to Anne in her room and says she was wrong
beats.summary: Marilla asks why Anne confessed, and then admits that she was wrong and apologises.

beats.scene: Children eat ice cream and row boats on a pond at the picnic
beats.summary: Anne goes to the picnic and has ice cream and a boat ride, the best day of her life.

beats.scene: Anne and Diana walk to school together under blue September skies
beats.summary: In September Anne starts school with Diana and feels excited and afraid.

beats.scene: A tall boy with curly brown hair grins at Anne across the school aisle
beats.summary: At school Anne notices Gilbert Blythe, a handsome boy who likes to tease the girls.

beats.scene: Gilbert tugs Anne's long red braid and whispers a name
beats.summary: Gilbert pulls Anne's braid and calls her Carrots in front of the class.

beats.scene: Anne brings her slate down on Gilbert's head, and it breaks
beats.summary: Anne is so furious that she hits Gilbert with her slate and breaks it clean in two.

beats.scene: Mr Phillips writes on the blackboard while Anne stands on the platform
beats.summary: Mr Phillips writes about Anne's temper on the board and makes her stand on the platform, and Gilbert apologises.

beats.scene: Anne sits at the kitchen table with arms folded, refusing to go back
beats.summary: Anne says that she will never go back to school while Mr Phillips and Gilbert are there.

beats.scene: Mrs Lynde and Marilla talk over their tea in the Green Gables kitchen
beats.summary: Mrs Lynde advises Marilla to let Anne stay at home for a while, and Anne misses her lessons.

beats.scene: Anne sits stiffly at her desk, looking straight ahead at the blackboard
beats.summary: Anne returns to school and refuses to speak to Gilbert, and a long rivalry begins.

beats.scene: Marilla leaves for a meeting while Anne waves from the garden gate
beats.summary: Marilla goes to a Ladies' Aid meeting and lets Anne invite Diana to tea.

beats.scene: Anne greets Diana at the door, playing the part of a grand hostess
beats.summary: Anne welcomes Diana like a grand lady, and the two girls enjoy playing at being grown up.

beats.scene: Anne pours a red drink from a bottle into tall glasses
beats.summary: Anne serves Diana what she thinks is raspberry cordial, and Diana drinks three glasses.

beats.scene: Diana sits pale and dizzy on a sofa and wants to go home
beats.summary: Diana begins to feel very ill, and she goes home unsteadily with Anne following in distress.

beats.scene: Mrs Barry stands stern at her door, with Diana behind her
beats.summary: Mrs Barry decides that Anne made Diana drunk on purpose and forbids the girls to play together again.

beats.scene: Marilla comes back from Orchard Slope looking annoyed and Anne weeps
beats.summary: Marilla explains the mistake to Mrs Barry, but Mrs Barry is unreasonable, and Anne is heartbroken.

beats.scene: Anne and Diana say a tearful goodbye in the dusk at the orchard fence
beats.summary: Anne and Diana say a sad goodbye and promise to be faithful for ever, though they must now meet only at school.

beats.scene: A young minister's wife with a kind smile greets Anne at church
beats.summary: Avonlea has a new minister, Mr Allan, and Anne loves his young wife at first sight.

beats.scene: Anne sits among girls in a Sunday school class, listening to Mrs Allan
beats.summary: Mrs Allan teaches Anne's Sunday school class and encourages the girls to ask questions.

beats.scene: Diana runs through the winter dusk to the door of Green Gables
beats.summary: One night Diana runs to Green Gables to say that her little sister Minnie May is very ill with croup.

beats.scene: Anne hurries into the Barry kitchen where a small child struggles to breathe
beats.summary: Anne remembers helping Mrs Hammond with her twins, and she goes to take charge of Minnie May.

beats.scene: Anne gives the medicine and works all night beside the little bed
beats.summary: Anne finds the syrup of ipecac and gives it again and again, working all night beside Minnie May.

beats.scene: Dr Spencer looks down at Minnie May asleep as the sun rises
beats.summary: The doctor arrives at dawn and says that Anne saved the little girl's life.

beats.scene: Mrs Barry holds Anne's hands in her parlour with tears in her eyes
beats.summary: Mrs Barry thanks Anne with tears in her eyes and says she was wrong about the wine.

beats.scene: Anne and Diana hug each other in a snowy garden, friends again
beats.summary: Mrs Barry lets Diana be friends with Anne again, and they are happier than ever.

beats.scene: Anne and Diana in a grand hall in Charlottetown, with lights and singers
beats.summary: Anne and Diana go to Charlottetown to a grand concert and stay with Diana's aunt.

beats.scene: Two girls leap into a bed and land on a startled old lady
beats.summary: Anne and Diana leap into the spare bed in the dark and land on Aunt Josephine, who is already asleep in it.

beats.scene: Anne comes home to Green Gables and Marilla greets her warmly
beats.summary: Anne apologises to Aunt Josephine and comes home, and Marilla admits she is glad to have her back.

beats.scene: Anne and Diana walk fearfully along a dark path between spruce trees
beats.summary: Anne and Diana invent ghost stories about a wood near the Barry farm, which they call the Haunted Wood.

beats.scene: Two girls race out of a wood at dusk, screaming with fright
beats.summary: One evening they imagine the ghost so clearly that they run out of the wood screaming.

beats.scene: Marilla scolds Anne in the kitchen while Anne holds her hands tight
beats.summary: Marilla says that Anne's imagination has gone too far, and she forbids the ghost stories.

beats.scene: Anne walks alone through the dark Haunted Wood with her heart pounding
beats.summary: Marilla sends Anne alone through the Haunted Wood at dusk to prove that there is nothing in it.

beats.scene: Anne stands at the kitchen window, planning a cake for the minister
beats.summary: Anne is delighted when Mrs Allan is to come to tea, and she decides to bake a layer cake.

beats.scene: Anne stirs a bowl of cake mixture, adding flavouring from a small bottle
beats.summary: While baking, Anne puts a bottle of liniment into the cake by mistake, thinking it is vanilla.

beats.scene: Mrs Allan lifts a forkful of cake as Anne watches eagerly
beats.summary: At tea Mrs Allan tastes the cake, and Anne realises that something is badly wrong.

beats.scene: Mrs Allan comforts Anne gently and says anyone can make a mistake
beats.summary: Mrs Allan comforts Anne kindly and says that the best of cakes can be spoiled by accident.

beats.scene: A group of girls gathers on a garden fence near a high farmhouse roof
beats.summary: At Orchard Slope, Anne and her friends play with Josie Pye, who dares Anne to walk the ridgepole of the roof.

beats.scene: Anne wobbles on a high roof ridge while friends stare up in horror
beats.summary: Anne walks along the ridgepole of the roof, loses her balance and falls to the ground.

beats.scene: Anne lies in bed with a bandaged ankle while Diana sits beside her
beats.summary: Anne hurts her ankle badly and has to stay in bed for weeks, though her friends visit to cheer her up.

beats.scene: A young teacher stands at the front of a bright schoolroom smiling
beats.summary: A new teacher, Miss Stacy, arrives at the Avonlea school, and the pupils like her at once.

beats.scene: Pupils walk in a wood with their teacher, looking at ferns and birds
beats.summary: Miss Stacy takes her pupils out to study nature and sets them to write their own compositions.

beats.scene: Children rehearse a play on the schoolroom platform while Miss Stacy directs
beats.summary: Miss Stacy plans a Christmas concert to raise money for a school flag, and Anne is given a recitation.

beats.scene: Anne stands on a hall stage in a white dress reciting to a crowd
beats.summary: At the concert in the hall Anne recites her poem, and the audience cheers.

beats.scene: Anne gazes at girls with puffed sleeves and sighs at her plain dress
beats.summary: At the concert Anne admires the girls with puffed sleeves and begs Marilla for a dress like theirs.

beats.scene: Matthew stands flustered in a shop, surrounded by shelves of cloth
beats.summary: Matthew goes into a shop to buy cloth for Anne's dress, but he is so shy that he nearly gives up.

beats.scene: Mrs Lynde sits at her sewing machine making a brown dress with sleeves
beats.summary: Matthew asks Mrs Lynde to make the dress, and she agrees to keep it secret from Anne.

beats.scene: Anne opens a parcel on Christmas morning and finds a dress with puffed sleeves
beats.summary: On Christmas morning Anne finds the dress, and Matthew's present makes her cry with joy.

beats.scene: Four girls sit under apple trees, reading stories aloud to each other
beats.summary: Anne starts a story club with Diana, Jane Andrews and Ruby Gillis, and each girl writes a story.

beats.scene: Mrs Allan smiles over a handful of Anne's pages at a garden table
beats.summary: Mrs Allan reads Anne's stories and kindly suggests that she write about things she knows.

beats.scene: A pedlar opens a case of bottles at the kitchen door
beats.summary: A pedlar comes to Green Gables with a bottle of hair dye that promises to turn red hair black.

beats.scene: Anne dips a comb into a bottle and stares into the mirror
beats.summary: Anne locks herself in her room and puts the dye on her hair, hoping to become a raven-haired beauty.

beats.scene: Anne screams at a mirror showing her hair as dull green
beats.summary: To Anne's horror, the dye turns her hair a dreadful shade of green.

beats.scene: Marilla gently cuts Anne's hair short with a pair of scissors
beats.summary: Marilla says the only cure is to cut off the green hair, and Anne promises never to be vain again.

beats.scene: Anne walks into school with short hair and meets amazed faces
beats.summary: Anne goes back to school with her short hair, and Diana tells her it does not matter.

beats.scene: Girls dress up as characters in a poem on the banks of a pond
beats.summary: Anne and her friends plan to act the story of the Lily Maid, with Anne as Elaine on a boat.

beats.scene: Anne lies in a leaking boat floating down a pond with water around her
beats.summary: Anne lies in the boat and floats down the pond, but the boat begins to leak.

beats.scene: Anne clings to a bridge post as a boy rows up to her
beats.summary: Anne climbs onto a pile under the bridge, and Gilbert Blythe rows up and rescues her.

beats.scene: Gilbert holds out his hand on the shore while Anne turns away
beats.summary: Gilbert asks Anne to be friends and says he is sorry about her hair, but she coldly refuses.

beats.scene: Anne sits alone on a bed in the evening, looking out at a pond
beats.summary: Later Anne secretly wishes that she had forgiven Gilbert, but she is too proud to say so.

beats.scene: Anne and Diana walk arm in arm along a lane of arching trees
beats.summary: In the spring Anne and Diana walk in Lover's Lane, sharing their dreams for the future.

beats.scene: Marilla looks up from her sewing at a taller Anne in the doorway
beats.summary: Anne grows tall and thin, and Marilla notices that she has become quieter and more serious.

beats.scene: Miss Stacy speaks to a small group of older pupils in the schoolroom
beats.summary: Miss Stacy forms a class to prepare the older pupils for the entrance examination to Queen's Academy.

beats.scene: Seven students sit at their desks in the early light with open books
beats.summary: Anne, Gilbert, Ruby, Jane, Josie, Charlie Sloane and Moody Spurgeon join the Queen's class.

beats.scene: Anne bends over a table of books, frowning at a diagram by lamplight
beats.summary: Anne studies Latin, algebra and geometry every evening, and she finds geometry the hardest.

beats.scene: Two students sit across a classroom, each bent over a paper
beats.summary: Anne and Gilbert compete for the best marks, though they still do not speak to each other.

beats.scene: Matthew sits down heavily on a chair in the kitchen, pale and tired
beats.summary: Matthew has a sudden attack of pain in his heart, and the doctor warns him to avoid heavy work and worry.

beats.scene: Anne stands by Matthew's chair promising to work harder than ever
beats.summary: Anne promises Matthew that she will work hard and make him proud of her.

beats.scene: Students step down from a train in a busy city street with bags
beats.summary: In June the Queen's class travels to Charlottetown to sit the entrance examination.

beats.scene: Anne frowns over a long examination paper in a quiet hall
beats.summary: Anne writes her papers and fears that she has failed geometry.

beats.scene: Anne and Diana sit on the porch steps in the long summer twilight
beats.summary: Back in Avonlea, Anne tells Diana that she is sure she has failed, and Diana comforts her.

beats.scene: Diana bursts into a room holding a newspaper over her head
beats.summary: Diana runs in with the newspaper and shouts that Anne has passed and is first, tied with Gilbert.

beats.scene: Anne stands with Matthew and Marilla in the kitchen, face glowing
beats.summary: Matthew and Marilla are proud, and Mrs Lynde and the neighbours come to offer their congratulations.

beats.scene: Anne looks at a hotel poster, a letter in her hand
beats.summary: Anne is asked to recite at a concert at the White Sands Hotel.

beats.scene: Anne stands in a white dress in front of a mirror, nervous and bright-eyed
beats.summary: On the night of the concert Anne wears a new white dress and feels very nervous among the grand ladies.

beats.scene: Anne recites on a bright stage while an audience listens in silence
beats.summary: Anne's turn comes, and she recites so well that the audience applauds.

beats.scene: Anne and Diana ride home under the stars in a buggy
beats.summary: Driving home under the stars, Anne tells Diana that the evening was wonderful but that she is glad to be going home.

beats.scene: Marilla sits at the table speaking to Anne about Queen's Academy
beats.summary: Marilla and Matthew decide to send Anne to Queen's Academy in the autumn.

beats.scene: A new trunk and dresses lie open on a bed in the east gable
beats.summary: Anne's new dresses are made and her trunk is packed, and she says goodbye to Diana.

beats.scene: Matthew drives Anne to the station while Marilla waves from the door
beats.summary: Matthew drives Anne to the station, and Marilla, who rarely shows her feelings, waves with tears in her eyes.

beats.scene: Anne stands in a crowded city boarding house, looking at a strange new room
beats.summary: Anne arrives in Charlottetown and feels lonely among crowds of strangers in her boarding house.

beats.scene: Students gather in a hall at Queen's Academy, listening to a notice
beats.summary: Anne hears about the Avery scholarship, which will pay for four years at Redmond College for the best student in English.

beats.scene: Anne leans over her books at a desk with a lamp, writing quickly
beats.summary: Anne works to finish two years of study in one winter, and she studies late into the night.

beats.scene: Anne steps off a train at a country station, where Matthew waits
beats.summary: Anne goes home to Green Gables on weekends, and Matthew meets her at the station.

beats.scene: Snow falls on a lit window of Green Gables on Christmas Eve
beats.summary: At Christmas Anne comes home and tells Marilla and Matthew about her life at the Academy.

beats.scene: Anne walks along a windy harbour front in Charlottetown in early spring
beats.summary: In the spring Anne walks by the harbour in Charlottetown and thinks about her future.

beats.scene: Students bend over examination papers in a silent hall in June
beats.summary: In June Anne sits her final examinations and hopes that she has done well.

beats.scene: Anne leaves a crowded school gate, hugging her books, as Gilbert watches
beats.summary: Anne says goodbye to the friends she has made and waits anxiously for the results.

beats.scene: Students crowd around a notice board in a school hall, cheering and pointing
beats.summary: The results are posted at Queen's, and Gilbert wins the gold medal while Anne wins the Avery scholarship.

beats.scene: Gilbert reaches out a hand to Anne in a crowded school hall
beats.summary: Gilbert warmly congratulates Anne, and she thanks him politely but notices that he is truly glad.

beats.scene: Anne rides a train past golden fields toward Avonlea, smiling at the window
beats.summary: Anne travels home by train, thinking of Green Gables and all the people who helped her.

beats.scene: Diana runs down the road to hug Anne as she steps from the buggy
beats.summary: At Green Gables Diana flings her arms around Anne, and Marilla serves all of Anne's favourite foods.

beats.scene: Matthew sits on the porch beside Anne in the warm evening light
beats.summary: That evening Matthew tells Anne that he would not exchange her for a dozen boys.

beats.scene: Anne takes Matthew's hand and smiles at him through her tears
beats.summary: Anne tells Matthew that she is glad he took her home, and Matthew smiles shyly.

beats.scene: Anne lies on the grass in the garden reading a letter from Redmond
beats.summary: In the summer Anne makes plans for her studies at Redmond, and Mrs Allan and the neighbours encourage her.

beats.scene: Anne and Diana sit side by side on a log at the Dryad's Bubble
beats.summary: Anne and Diana talk about the day Anne must leave for Redmond and promise that they will always be friends.

beats.scene: Matthew rests on a kitchen chair, looking old and tired
beats.summary: Matthew grows more tired, and Marilla notices that he works less and rests more.

beats.scene: Anne sits at her east gable window in the moonlight, looking at the orchard
beats.summary: On a quiet evening Anne sits by her window and thanks God for Green Gables and for all her friends.

beats.scene: Marilla and Matthew talk quietly at the kitchen table over a small notebook
beats.summary: Matthew's savings are all in the Abbey Bank, and Marilla begs him to be careful about the rumours.

beats.scene: Anne sits beside Matthew on the porch, speaking of Redmond in the dusk
beats.summary: In the evening Anne tells Matthew about the books she hopes to read at Redmond, and he listens proudly.

beats.scene: A newspaper lies on a kitchen table beside a lamp and an empty chair
beats.summary: A few days later the newspaper brings the news that the Abbey Bank has failed.

beats.scene: Marilla looks up from her knitting as Matthew sits down with the paper
beats.summary: Matthew tells Marilla that the bank has failed, and Marilla says that nothing can be done.

beats.scene: Anne walks home through the dusk with a bunch of white flowers
beats.summary: Anne returns from Diana's at dusk and sees Matthew standing at the door with the newspaper in his hand.

beats.scene: Anne reaches for Matthew's arm as his newspaper slips to the ground
beats.summary: Matthew sways and falls, and Anne cries out for Marilla.

beats.scene: Two women kneel beside a still figure while a neighbour hurries away for help
beats.summary: Marilla and Anne carry Matthew inside, and a neighbour hurries to fetch the doctor.

beats.scene: The doctor speaks gently to Marilla beside a sofa in a silent room
beats.summary: The doctor says that Matthew died instantly of heart failure, brought on by the shock, and felt no pain.

beats.scene: Anne sits silent at a kitchen window while Mrs Lynde takes charge
beats.summary: Anne is too stunned to weep, while Mrs Lynde comes to help and takes charge of the house.

beats.scene: Anne picks white roses from an old bush in the garden at dawn
beats.summary: At dawn Anne picks Matthew's favourite white roses from the old bush to lay beside him.

beats.scene: A long line of mourners follows a coffin down a country lane
beats.summary: The whole village comes to Matthew's funeral, and Mr Allan speaks a few kind words.

beats.scene: Neighbours stand in a green churchyard, heads bowed beside an open grave
beats.summary: At the graveside the neighbours say that Matthew was the kindest and shyest man in Avonlea.

beats.scene: Anne walks alone through the quiet rooms of Green Gables at twilight
beats.summary: After the funeral Anne wanders through the silent house and sees Matthew's chair, his hat and his boots.

beats.scene: Anne sits in the garden and laughs at something, then stops, ashamed
beats.summary: Anne finds herself smiling at the sunset and feels guilty that she can be happy when Matthew is gone.

beats.scene: Anne lies on her bed at night, crying into her pillow at last
beats.summary: At night Anne's tears come at last, and she weeps for the man who first welcomed her home.

beats.scene: Marilla sits on the edge of Anne's bed in the dark, holding her
beats.summary: Marilla comes in and holds Anne close, and she tells her that she loves her as her own daughter.

beats.scene: Marilla and Anne sit close together at the kitchen table by lamplight
beats.summary: Marilla admits that she was never good at showing her feelings and says Matthew was wiser than she was.

beats.scene: Anne reads a letter from Redmond at a table, frowning slowly
beats.summary: The days pass, and Anne must decide whether she will go to Redmond College in the autumn.

beats.scene: Marilla looks at an empty cash box and a small pile of papers
beats.summary: Marilla explains that Matthew's savings are gone and that the farm is hard to run without him.

beats.scene: Marilla stands with her hand over her eyes, pale and worried
beats.summary: Marilla's headaches grow worse and her sight begins to fail, so she decides to see a specialist in Charlottetown.

beats.scene: Marilla sits very still in the kitchen, her hands folded, speaking quietly
beats.summary: The specialist tells Marilla that she must give up reading and sewing and avoid crying, or she may go blind.

beats.scene: Marilla looks round the kitchen with a heavy heart, speaking of selling
beats.summary: Marilla says that she cannot manage the farm alone, and she thinks she must sell Green Gables.

beats.scene: Anne sits at her window in the moonlight, deep in thought, unable to sleep
beats.summary: Anne lies awake all night, thinking of Marilla, Matthew and what she owes them.

beats.scene: Anne comes down in the morning, calm and steady, with a smile for Marilla
beats.summary: In the morning Anne tells Marilla that she has decided to give up the scholarship and stay at Green Gables.

beats.scene: Marilla shakes her head at Anne across the table, tears in her eyes
beats.summary: Marilla says she cannot let Anne give up her future, but Anne insists, and Marilla gives way with tears.

beats.scene: Anne explains a plan by the kitchen fire, counting on her fingers
beats.summary: Anne explains that she will teach at a school nearby and study at home, and that Marilla will not be alone.

beats.scene: Anne talks to Mr Barry in a field of tall grass, beside a fence
beats.summary: Mr Barry agrees to rent the Green Gables fields, and Anne tells him that she will keep the house.

beats.scene: Diana and Anne hug each other beside a garden gate in the dusk
beats.summary: Anne tells Diana, who is so glad that Anne is staying that she cries for joy.

beats.scene: Mrs Lynde bustles up the lane of Green Gables with important news
beats.summary: Mrs Lynde brings news that the trustees have given the Avonlea school to Gilbert Blythe, who has given it up for Anne.

beats.scene: Anne stops on a path under the autumn trees, thinking of Gilbert
beats.summary: Anne is astonished by Gilbert's kindness and decides that she must thank him.

beats.scene: Anne and Gilbert meet on a quiet road at sunset and stop
beats.summary: Anne meets Gilbert on the road and thanks him for giving up the school, and he says they were meant to be friends.

beats.scene: Anne and Gilbert walk side by side down the lane under autumn leaves
beats.summary: Gilbert says that they were born to be good friends, and Anne agrees and says she is sorry about the long quarrel.

beats.scene: Marilla looks out of a lamplit window as Anne comes up the path
beats.summary: Marilla remarks on Gilbert and tells Anne that she once quarrelled with his father and never forgave him.

beats.scene: Anne stands before a class of children in a country school at autumn
beats.summary: In the autumn Anne begins to teach at the Avonlea school, and she is determined to be patient and kind.

beats.scene: Anne reads aloud to Marilla by the lamp as snow begins to fall
beats.summary: In the evenings Anne reads aloud to Marilla, whose eyesight stops getting worse.

beats.scene: Anne and Diana walk arm in arm under bare branches talking happily
beats.summary: Anne and Diana remain the closest of friends, and they walk together and talk about all that lies ahead of them.

beats.scene: Anne smiles at a small pupil who has finished a hard lesson
beats.summary: Anne finds that she loves teaching, and that she remembers how it felt to be a child who was not understood.

beats.scene: Anne kneels at a small grave beneath a white rose bush in the evening
beats.summary: Anne visits Matthew's grave, lays flowers there and promises him that she will be a good daughter to Marilla.

beats.scene: Anne walks home along a country road in the golden evening
beats.summary: Anne walks home from the churchyard, and she thinks about her life and how much has changed since she first came.

beats.scene: Anne stands where the road bends, looking at the golden evening ahead
beats.summary: Anne stops where the road bends, and she feels hopeful about what lies beyond it, for she knows that the best is yet to come.

A1A2: Mrs Rachel Lynde lived beside the road and watched everyone who passed.
Matthew Cuthbert drove by in his best clothes, and Mrs Lynde was surprised.
After tea, Mrs Lynde walked up to Green Gables to ask Marilla.
Marilla said a boy from an orphan home was coming on the train.
Mrs Lynde was shocked and said it was a very risky thing to do.
Marilla said Matthew was old, his heart was weak, and help was hard to find.
Matthew drove eight miles in the soft evening light.
Matthew felt shy with women, so he hoped the boy would be easy.
At Bright River the train had gone, and only a small girl was there.
The man at the station said the little girl was waiting for Matthew.
Anne jumped up and said she was glad that Matthew had come.
She was thin, with long red hair and a pale, spotted face.
Matthew helped her into the buggy, and Anne began to talk.
Anne called the road of white apple trees the White Way of Delight.
At the pond Anne said it needed a better name too.
Anne asked why the roads were red, but Matthew did not know.
Anne said no one had ever wanted her, and she hoped for a friend.
Matthew was not used to talk, but he liked listening to Anne.
Marilla opened the door and saw a strange little girl.
Anne understood the mistake and began to cry loudly.
Marilla and Matthew looked at each other while Anne cried.
Anne was too sad to eat, and she asked Marilla to call her Cordelia.
Marilla took Anne to a small room, and Anne cried herself to sleep.
Marilla said the girl must go back, but Matthew was not sure.
In the morning Anne saw a big cherry tree outside her window.
Anne sat at the table and said she was too sad to eat.
Anne said her parents had died when she was only three months old.
Anne worked for Mrs Thomas and then for Mrs Hammond, who had many children.
Anne told Marilla about her imaginary friends and her lonely days.
Matthew told Marilla that he would like to keep Anne.
Marilla took Anne to see Mrs Spencer, and Anne enjoyed the drive.
Mrs Spencer was very surprised that the Cuthberts had wanted a boy.
A hard woman, Mrs Blewett, came and looked at Anne carefully.
Marilla did not like Mrs Blewett, so she took Anne home.
On the way home Marilla told Anne she could stay if she was good.
Anne did not know how to pray, and Marilla was shocked.
Anne said a prayer in her own words, and Marilla listened.
Marilla gave Anne a prayer to learn and made rules for her.
Marilla gave Anne some sewing, but Anne did not like it.
Mrs Lynde had been ill, and now she came to see the child.
Mrs Lynde looked at Anne for a long time and was not kind.
She said Anne was thin and plain, with hair as red as a carrot.
Anne lost her temper and stamped her foot at Mrs Lynde.
Marilla sent Anne to her room, and Mrs Lynde went home angry.
Anne stayed in her room, and Marilla said she must say sorry.
Matthew came quietly to Anne's room and said she should say sorry.
Anne got on her knees before Mrs Lynde and said she was sorry.
Mrs Lynde was kind to Anne and said her hair might get darker.
On Sunday Anne put wild flowers on her hat and went to church.
At church people looked at Anne's hat, but she loved the singing.
Marilla said a hat with wild flowers was not right for church.
Marilla sent Anne to Orchard Slope, and she felt nervous.
Anne met Diana Barry, a pretty girl with dark hair and bright eyes.
Anne asked Diana to be her best friend for all of her life.
The two girls promised to be best friends for ever and ever.
Anne came home full of joy because she had a best friend.
Anne and Diana played in the woods and named all of their favourite places.
Anne could think of nothing but the picnic with the Sunday school.
On Monday Marilla could not find her best purple pin.
Anne said she had tried on the pin but put it back.
Anne wanted to go to the picnic, so she told a story.
Marilla was very angry and said that Anne could not go.
On picnic morning Marilla found her pin in her black wrap.
Marilla said she was sorry, and Anne said it was all right.
At the picnic Anne ate ice cream and rode in a boat.
In September Anne started school with Diana.
In school there was a tall boy named Gilbert Blythe.
Gilbert pulled Anne's hair and called her Carrots.
Anne hit Gilbert with her slate, and the slate broke.
Mr Phillips made Anne stand in front of the whole class.
Anne said she would never go back to school again.
Mrs Lynde said that Anne could stay at home for a while.
Anne went back to school, but she did not speak to Gilbert.
Marilla went to a meeting and let Anne invite Diana to tea.
Anne welcomed Diana as if she were a grand lady.
Anne gave Diana a red drink, and Diana had three glasses.
Diana felt ill, and she went home feeling very strange.
Mrs Barry was angry and said Diana must not see Anne again.
Marilla tried to help, but Mrs Barry would not listen.
Anne and Diana said goodbye and promised to be faithful.
A new minister came to Avonlea, and Anne loved his wife.
Mrs Allan taught the girls, and Anne asked many questions.
One night Diana ran to Green Gables because her sister was ill.
Anne remembered the twins, and she hurried to help the little girl.
Anne gave the child medicine, and she worked through the night.
At dawn the doctor came and said that Anne had saved Minnie May.
Mrs Barry thanked Anne and said she was sorry about the wine.
Diana could play with Anne again, and they were very happy.
Anne and Diana went to a big concert in the city.
The girls jumped into bed in the dark and landed on Aunt Josephine.
Anne said sorry and went home, and Marilla was glad.
Anne and Diana made up ghost stories about a dark wood.
One night they ran out of the wood, afraid of the ghost.
Marilla was angry and said there would be no more ghost stories.
Marilla sent Anne through the wood alone to prove there was no ghost.
Mrs Allan was coming to tea, and Anne planned to bake a cake.
While baking, Anne put the wrong bottle into the cake.
Mrs Allan tasted the cake, and Anne saw that something was wrong.
Mrs Allan was kind and said that anyone could make a mistake.
Josie Pye dared Anne to walk on top of the roof.
Anne walked on the roof, lost her balance, and fell.
Anne hurt her ankle, and she had to stay in bed for weeks.
A new teacher, Miss Stacy, came, and the children liked her.
Miss Stacy took the children outside to learn about nature.
Miss Stacy planned a concert, and Anne had a poem to learn.
At the concert, Anne said her poem, and the people cheered.
Anne wanted a dress with puffed sleeves like the other girls.
Matthew went into a shop to buy cloth, but he was too shy.
Matthew asked Mrs Lynde to make the dress, and she agreed.
On Christmas morning Anne found the dress and cried with joy.
Anne and her friends started a club to write stories.
Mrs Allan told Anne to write about things she knew well.
A man came to the door with a bottle for dyeing hair.
Anne went to her room and put the dye on her hair.
In the mirror Anne saw that her hair was green.
Marilla cut off Anne's hair, and Anne learned a lesson.
Anne went to school with short hair, and Diana was kind.
The girls planned to play a story, and Anne was the Lily Maid.
Anne lay in the boat, but water began to come in.
Gilbert rowed to Anne in his boat and took her to land.
Gilbert asked Anne to be friends, but she said no.
Later Anne was sorry that she had not been kinder to Gilbert.
In spring Anne and Diana walked together and shared their dreams.
Anne grew taller, and Marilla saw that she was changing.
Miss Stacy made a class for the older pupils who wanted to be teachers.
Seven pupils joined the class, and Anne and Gilbert were two of them.
Anne studied hard every evening, but some lessons were very hard.
Anne and Gilbert both worked hard, and they did not speak.
Matthew had a pain in his chest, and the doctor came.
Anne told Matthew that she would work hard and make him proud.
In June the class went to Charlottetown for the big examination.
Anne wrote her papers, but she was afraid she had failed one.
At home Anne told Diana that she was sure she had failed.
Diana ran in with the newspaper and cried that Anne had passed.
Matthew and Marilla were proud of Anne, and the neighbours came.
Anne was asked to say a poem at a concert at the hotel.
On the night, Anne put on a white dress and felt nervous.
Anne said her poem, and the people clapped for a long time.
Anne and Diana drove home under the stars and talked happily.
Marilla and Matthew said that Anne could go to Queen's in the autumn.
Anne's new clothes were ready, and she said goodbye to Diana.
Matthew drove Anne to the station, and Marilla wept.
In the city Anne felt lonely among all the strangers.
Anne heard about a prize that would pay for college.
Anne worked hard to finish two years of study in one winter.
On weekends Anne went home, and Matthew met her at the station.
At Christmas Anne came home and told them about her studies.
In spring Anne walked by the sea and thought about her future.
In June Anne took her last tests and hoped she had done well.
Anne said goodbye to her friends and waited for the results.
At Queen's, Gilbert won the gold medal, and Anne won the scholarship.
Gilbert told Anne he was glad, and she thanked him.
Anne went home on the train, thinking of Green Gables.
At home Diana hugged Anne, and Marilla made Anne's favourite food.
That evening Matthew said he would not trade Anne for a dozen boys.
Anne told Matthew she was glad he had brought her home.
In summer Anne made plans for her studies at Redmond.
Anne and Diana promised to stay best friends for ever.
Matthew seemed more tired, and Marilla began to worry about him.
One evening Anne sat at her window and was thankful for everything.
Matthew's money was in the Abbey Bank, and Marilla was afraid.
Anne told Matthew about Redmond, and he listened proudly.
A few days later the newspaper said that the Abbey Bank had failed.
Matthew told Marilla the bank had failed, and she was calm.
Anne came home from Diana's and saw Matthew at the door.
Matthew fell to the ground, and Anne cried for help.
They carried Matthew inside, and someone ran for the doctor.
The doctor said that Matthew had died quickly without pain.
Anne was too shocked to cry, and Mrs Lynde came to help.
At dawn Anne picked Matthew's favourite white roses for him.
The whole village came to Matthew's funeral and spoke kindly of him.
At the grave the neighbours said that Matthew was kind and shy.
After the funeral the house felt empty, and Anne walked through it.
Anne smiled at the sunset, and then she felt guilty.
At night Anne began to cry, and she cried for a long time.
Marilla held Anne close and said that she loved her very much.
Marilla said that Matthew had been wiser than she was.
Days passed, and Anne had to decide about college.
Marilla said that the money was gone and the farm was hard to run.
Marilla's eyes grew worse, so she went to see a doctor in the city.
The eye doctor told Marilla to stop reading and sewing.
Marilla said she could not run the farm alone, so she must sell it.
Anne could not sleep, and she thought about Marilla all night.
In the morning Anne said that she would stay and give up the scholarship.
Marilla said no at first, but at last she gave way and cried.
Anne said she would teach at a school near home.
Mr Barry agreed to rent the fields at Green Gables.
Diana was very glad that Anne was staying, and she cried.
Mrs Lynde said that Gilbert had given up the Avonlea school for Anne.
Anne was surprised that Gilbert was so kind, and she wanted to thank him.
Anne met Gilbert on the road and thanked him for his kindness.
Gilbert said they were meant to be friends, and Anne agreed.
Marilla told Anne about a quarrel she once had with Gilbert's father.
In autumn Anne began to teach at the Avonlea school.
In the evenings Anne read aloud to Marilla by the lamp.
Anne and Diana stayed close friends, and they made plans together.
Anne loved teaching, and she was kind to every child.
Anne visited Matthew's grave and promised to take care of Marilla.
Anne walked home and thought about how much her life had changed.
Anne stopped at the bend in the road, and she felt full of hope.
B1B2: Mrs Rachel Lynde lives where the main road of Avonlea dips into a hollow and a small brook runs through. From her window she sees every cart and buggy go by, and nothing on the road escapes her.

Matthew Cuthbert, the shyest man in Avonlea, drives past in his buggy with a white collar and his best suit. He never goes anywhere in the middle of the working week, so Mrs Lynde is sure that something important is happening.

After tea, Mrs Lynde walks up the lane to Green Gables, a farmhouse that stands in an orchard, far back from the road. She finds Marilla Cuthbert, a tall, thin woman whose dark hair is streaked with grey, sitting in the tidy kitchen.

Marilla explains that Mrs Spencer has chosen a boy at the orphan asylum in Hopetown, and that he is arriving on the evening train. Matthew has driven to Bright River station to meet him, because the Cuthberts mean to adopt him.
Mrs Lynde is so shocked that she can hardly speak, and then she says that Marilla is taking a terrible risk. She has heard stories of orphan boys who set fire to houses and put poison in the well.
Marilla answers that Matthew is about sixty now, and his heart troubles him a good deal. Hired men are hard to find, and a boy who is brought up properly could soon become a real help.

Matthew enjoys the long drive to Bright River, because the orchards are in bloom and the air smells sweet. On the island you must nod to everyone you meet, whether you know them or not, and he does it politely.
Matthew is afraid of every woman he meets, except his sister and Mrs Lynde. He hopes the boy will be a cheerful, sensible fellow whom he can talk to without any trouble.
Matthew arrives at Bright River station and finds the long platform nearly empty, because the train came in early. He sees no boy anywhere, only a small girl sitting alone on a pile of shingles.

The stationmaster tells him that a child was left at the station for Mr Cuthbert, and he points to the girl on the shingles. She refused to wait in the ladies' room, he adds, because she said there was more room for imagination outside.
Matthew is about to speak when the girl springs up and holds out a thin brown hand. She says she is glad to see him and was ready to sleep in a cherry tree if he had not come.

She wears a short, tight dress of yellowish grey and a faded brown sailor hat, and two thick red braids hang down her back. Her face is small, white and freckled, and her large eyes seem to change colour with her mood.
Matthew lifts her into the buggy, and the mare turns toward home. Anne begins to talk at once, and she hardly stops for breath, so Matthew has no chance to tell her about the mistake.

The road runs under a long arch of apple trees, and the blossoms hang over them like a white roof. Anne is so delighted that she says the place needs a better name, and she calls it the White Way of Delight.
When they pass a large pond, Matthew tells her that it is called Barry's Pond. Anne does not like the name at all, and she decides that she will call it the Lake of Shining Waters.

Anne has been told that Prince Edward Island is lovely, and she asks why its roads are red. Matthew has no idea, but she is not troubled, because she thinks it is wonderful to have so much left to find out.

Anne tells Matthew that she has never really belonged to anybody, so it is wonderful to be going to a home of her own. She hopes to find a bosom friend near Green Gables, and Matthew mentions Diana Barry.
Matthew has never heard so many words in one evening, and he is a little dizzy. Yet he finds, to his surprise, that he does not mind, because the strange child is so cheerful and honest.
It is nearly dark when they reach the lane of Green Gables, and a lamp shines in the kitchen window. Marilla opens the door, looks at the girl beside Matthew, and asks him where the boy is.
Marilla says there must be some mistake, because they asked for a boy. Anne understands that she is not wanted, and she bursts into tears.
Marilla asks Matthew what he was thinking, and he says that he could not leave a child at the station in the dark. She tells Anne that there is no need to cry so much, but Anne cannot stop.
Marilla gives the girl supper, but she is far too unhappy to eat. When Marilla asks her name, she begs to be called Cordelia, although her real name is Anne Shirley.
Marilla leads the tired girl upstairs to the little room in the east gable and leaves her a candle. The room is very clean and very bare, and Anne cries into her pillow until she falls asleep.

Downstairs, Marilla says that Mrs Spencer will have to take the child back, because a girl is no use to them. Matthew says only that she is a nice little thing, and that it seems a pity to send her away.
In the morning Anne wakes in a flood of sunshine and runs to the window. A huge cherry tree, white with blossom, brushes against the glass, and beyond it she sees an orchard and a garden.
At breakfast Anne is very quiet at first, and then she says she is in the depths of despair. She asks Marilla if she could eat in such a state, and Marilla replies that she has never tried.
Anne tells Marilla that she was born in Bolingbroke in Nova Scotia, and that her father was a teacher named Walter Shirley. Both her parents died of fever when she was only three months old.

Anne explains that she worked at Mrs Thomas's house and looked after her four children until Mr Thomas was killed by a train. Then she lived with Mrs Hammond, who had eight children, including three pairs of twins.
Anne spent four months at the asylum, and she says she was often lonely. To keep herself company she imagined friends, Katie Maurice in the glass of a bookcase and Violetta, the echo in the woods.
Marilla sends Anne outside to look at the garden, and she is quiet for a while. Then Matthew says, in his slow way, that he would rather like to keep the child.
That afternoon Marilla drives Anne to White Sands to ask Mrs Spencer what should be done. Anne is frightened, but she decides to enjoy the drive, because it may be her last.
Mrs Spencer is astonished to hear that the Cuthberts wanted a boy, because she thought they had asked for a girl. She says that somebody must have muddled the message, and she is very sorry.
While they are talking, Mrs Peter Blewett arrives and says she is looking for a girl to help with her children. She looks Anne up and down, and Marilla does not like her sharp face.
Marilla cannot bear the thought of leaving a child with such a woman. She tells Mrs Spencer that she will take Anne home again and talk to Matthew.
On the drive home Marilla says that she and Matthew will keep Anne, as long as she behaves herself and tries to be good. Anne is so happy that she can hardly speak, which is a rare thing for her.

That night Marilla tells Anne to say her prayers, and she is shocked to find that the girl has never learned any. Anne says that Mrs Thomas told her God made her hair red on purpose, and that she has not cared for Him since.

Anne prays in her own words, and she thanks God for the White Way of Delight, the Lake of Shining Waters and the Snow Queen. She asks to stay at Green Gables and to be pretty, and she ends politely with her full name.
Marilla tells Anne that she must learn a proper prayer, and Anne agrees at once. Marilla also tells her the rules of the house: she must be tidy, she must be useful, and she must do as she is told.
Marilla gives Anne a basket of pieces to sew into a patchwork quilt. Anne says there is no scope for imagination in plain squares, and she finds the work dull and slow.
Two weeks after Anne's arrival, Mrs Lynde comes to Green Gables at last, because she has been ill in bed. She has heard all about the girl from other people, and she wants to see Anne for herself.
Mrs Lynde sits down in the kitchen and looks Anne up and down for a long time. She tells Marilla that the girl certainly was not chosen for her looks.
Mrs Lynde says that Anne is terribly skinny and plain, and that her freckles are dreadful. She adds that her hair is as red as carrots, and she says it quite cheerfully.
Anne's temper explodes, and she stamps her foot and shouts that she hates Mrs Lynde. She says it is rude and cruel to talk about a girl like that, and she asks how Mrs Lynde would like it.
Marilla tells Anne to go to her room and stay there until she is called. Mrs Lynde leaves in a huff, saying that Marilla will have her hands full with such a bad-tempered child.
Anne lies on her bed and cries for a long time, and she refuses to come down for her meals. Marilla says that she may stay there until she is ready to apologise to Mrs Lynde.
Matthew, who hates trouble, climbs the stairs on tiptoe to talk to Anne. He tells her gently that she had better apologise to Mrs Lynde, because Marilla is very firm.
Anne agrees, and she walks to Mrs Lynde's house and kneels on the kitchen floor. She makes a long, dramatic apology and says that she is the wickedest girl in the world.
Mrs Lynde forgives her at once, and she says that she was perhaps too outspoken herself. She remembers a girl at school whose red hair grew into a lovely auburn, so Anne's may do the same.
On Sunday morning Anne trims her plain hat with buttercups and wild roses, and she thinks it looks beautiful. She walks to church in it, quite sure that everyone will admire it.
At church the neighbours stare at the flowery hat, and some of them smile behind their hands. Anne does not notice, because she loves the singing, though she finds the sermon very long.
Marilla tells Anne that a hat full of wild flowers is not right for church, and that people were laughing. Anne is sorry, but she is glad that she had no idea, because she enjoyed it so much.
One afternoon Marilla sends Anne to Orchard Slope, the Barrys' farm, to borrow a pattern from Mrs Barry. Anne walks there through the woods, wondering whether the girl who lives there will like her.
In the garden Anne sees a pretty girl with black hair, rosy cheeks and merry eyes. This is Diana Barry, and she smiles shyly at the strange red-haired girl.
Anne asks Diana, very seriously, whether she thinks she could like her enough to be her bosom friend. Diana laughs, because she has been told that the new girl at Green Gables is a little odd.
Anne says that they must swear an oath, and Diana agrees. Holding hands, they promise to be faithful friends for as long as the sun and moon endure, and Diana thinks the words are lovely.
Anne runs home through the woods, so happy that her feet hardly touch the ground. She tells Marilla that she has found a bosom friend at last, and that her name is Diana.

Every free hour Anne and Diana play together in the woods near Green Gables. Anne gives names to the places they love, such as the Dryad's Bubble for the spring and Violet Vale for the hollow of flowers.

Marilla tells Anne that the Sunday school picnic will be held on Wednesday, and she is allowed to go. Anne talks about nothing else, because she has never been to a picnic and has never tasted ice cream.
On Monday evening Marilla goes to her room and finds that her amethyst brooch is gone from the pincushion. It belonged to her mother, and she values it above everything else she owns.
Marilla asks Anne whether she has seen the brooch, and Anne says that she went into the room and tried it on. She says she put it back, but Marilla thinks she is not telling the truth.
Anne wants so much to go to the picnic that she decides to give Marilla the confession she asks for. She makes up a long story that she took the brooch and dropped it in the Lake of Shining Waters.
Marilla is shocked and angry, because Anne seems to have taken the brooch and lost it. She says that Anne cannot go to the picnic, and that she must stay in her room.

On the morning of the picnic, Marilla takes out her black shawl and finds her brooch hanging in the fringe. She remembers that she pinned it there herself, and she realises that Anne had told the truth.
Marilla goes upstairs and asks Anne why she made up the story, and Anne says that Marilla wanted her to confess. Marilla admits that she was wrong to force the girl, and she says that she is sorry.
Anne hurries to the picnic and spends a wonderful afternoon with the other children. She tastes ice cream for the first time and goes out in a boat, and she says it was the happiest day of her life.
In September Anne starts school at last, and she walks there with Diana along the road under the trees. She is excited and a little afraid, because she has never been in a proper class before.
At school Anne notices a tall boy named Gilbert Blythe, who has curly brown hair and merry hazel eyes. He loves to tease the girls, and he decides to find out what the new girl is like.
Mr Phillips is busy at the back of the room when Gilbert reaches over and pulls Anne's braid. He whispers Carrots, so that all the class can hear, and the children begin to giggle.
Anne jumps up and brings her slate down hard on Gilbert's head, so that it cracks across. The room goes dead silent, and Gilbert sits with his mouth open and does not say a word.
Mr Phillips writes a notice about Anne's bad temper on the blackboard, and he makes her stand on the platform all afternoon. Later Gilbert says he is sorry, but Anne refuses even to look at him.
At home Anne says that she will never go back to school, and she is very stubborn about it. Marilla is annoyed, but she does not know how to make her go.
Mrs Lynde tells Marilla to let Anne have her way for a while, because she will soon grow tired of staying home. Anne misses Diana and her lessons, and Diana comes to see her every afternoon.
At last Anne goes back to school, and she does not look at Gilbert once. She works so hard at her lessons that she is soon at the top of the class, and Gilbert works hard to beat her.

One afternoon Marilla goes to a meeting of the Ladies' Aid Society, and she says that Anne may invite Diana to tea. She tells her where to find the cake and the raspberry cordial, and she warns her to be careful.
Diana arrives in her second-best dress and knocks politely at the door. Anne plays the part of a grand lady, and the two girls talk about the weather and their gardens like grown women.
Anne fetches the bottle from the shelf and pours the red drink into two tall glasses. Diana finds it delicious and drinks three glasses of it, never guessing that the bottle held wine.
After a while Diana begins to feel dizzy and sick, and she says that she must go home. She walks away unsteadily, and Anne watches her go with a frightened heart.
Mrs Barry finds that her daughter has been drinking wine, and she is furious. She decides that Anne did it on purpose, and she says that Diana may never play with her again.
Marilla finds the wine bottle and knows that it was an honest mistake, so she goes to explain it to Mrs Barry. She comes home annoyed, because Mrs Barry would not listen, and Anne is very unhappy.
Anne meets Diana at the edge of the orchard, and they say a sad goodbye. They promise always to be faithful to each other, although they will meet only at school from now on.
Avonlea gets a new minister, Mr Allan, and his young wife comes to the village with him. Anne takes one look at Mrs Allan's kind face and loves her at once.
Mrs Allan teaches Anne's Sunday school class, and she lets the girls ask any question they like. Anne asks more questions than anyone else, and Mrs Allan always answers her patiently.
One winter night Diana runs in a panic to Green Gables, for her little sister Minnie May is very ill. She has the croup, and Diana's parents are away from home.
Anne tells Marilla that she knows about croup, because Mrs Hammond's twins had it three times. She hurries to the Barry house and finds Minnie May hot and fighting for each breath.
Anne finds a bottle of medicine in the cupboard and gives it to the little girl, again and again. She stays beside the bed through the long night and never stops trying.
Minnie May's breathing slowly improves, and she falls asleep just as the doctor arrives at dawn. He says that the girl has saved the child's life, and he tells Anne that she should go home to rest.
Mrs Barry comes to Green Gables and thanks Anne warmly, with tears in her eyes. She says that she was wrong to think that the wine was no accident, and she asks Anne to forgive her.
From that day Mrs Barry lets Diana be friends with Anne again. The two girls are happier than ever, and they promise never to be parted by anyone.

Diana's family invites Anne to go to a concert in Charlottetown, and they will stay with Diana's rich old aunt, Miss Josephine Barry. The concert is grand, and Anne is delighted by the lights and the music.
That night the two excited girls race to the spare bed in the dark and jump into it together. Aunt Josephine is already asleep there, and she wakes up shouting and very angry indeed.
Anne apologises to Miss Barry, who is still stiff but not unkind, and the girls go home. Marilla is glad to see her, and says that the house was lonely without her.
Near Orchard Slope there is a dark wood of spruce trees, and Anne and Diana call it the Haunted Wood. They invent a ghost story about it, and each night they tell it with more details.
One evening at dusk they walk through the wood and imagine the ghost so clearly that they scream. They run all the way home and burst into the kitchen, white with terror.

Marilla tells Anne that her imagination has gone far too far, and that she will not have any more of this foolish ghost nonsense. She says that Anne must stop at once, and that she must promise never to do it again.
To cure Anne, Marilla sends her through the Haunted Wood alone at dusk on an errand. Anne trembles with fear all the way, but she sees nothing at all, and she runs home safe.
Mr and Mrs Allan are coming to tea at Green Gables, and Anne is thrilled. She asks Marilla to let her bake a layer cake, because she wants everything to be perfect for Mrs Allan.
Anne bakes the cake carefully, and it rises beautifully. When she adds the flavouring, she takes the wrong bottle from the shelf, and she pours liniment into the cake, thinking it is vanilla.
At tea Anne watches eagerly as Mrs Allan takes a bite of the cake. Her face changes, and Anne tastes a piece herself and realises that the cake is horrible.
Mrs Allan puts her arm around the sobbing girl and says that it was an honest mistake. She says she is sure Anne did her best, and she asks to see her flower garden after tea.
One afternoon Anne and her friends are playing in the Barry garden, and Josie Pye dares Anne to walk along the roof. Anne has never refused a dare in her life, and she cannot start now.
Anne climbs up and begins to walk along the top of the roof, but halfway across she loses her balance. She slides off the roof and falls hard to the ground, and her friends scream.
Anne is carried home with a badly hurt ankle, and she has to stay in bed for many weeks. Diana and Mrs Allan come to visit, and Anne decides that she will never accept a dare again.
When Anne returns to school, there is a new teacher, a young woman called Miss Stacy. She is clever and kind, and Anne and all the girls love her at once.
Miss Stacy takes the pupils on walks in the woods to learn about birds, flowers and trees. She also asks them to write their own compositions, and Anne finds that she loves to write.
Miss Stacy decides to hold a concert to raise money for a flag for the school. Anne is given a poem to recite, and she practises it everywhere she goes.

On the night of the concert, the hall is full, and Anne stands on the stage in front of everyone. She forgets her fear as soon as she begins to recite, and the audience claps loudly when she finishes.
Anne has noticed that all the other girls are wearing dresses with puffed sleeves, and she wants one very badly. Marilla says that the fashion is silly and she will not hear of it.
Matthew makes up his mind to buy Anne the dress, and he goes into a shop. A young woman is serving, and he is so shy that he buys things he does not need before he dares to ask.
Matthew cannot sew, so he asks Mrs Lynde to make the dress. She agrees at once, and she promises to keep the secret and to give it big puffed sleeves.
On Christmas morning Anne finds a parcel at her door, and inside is a beautiful brown dress with puffed sleeves. She cries with joy, and she hugs Matthew and tells him it is the loveliest present.
Anne starts a story club with Diana, Jane Andrews and Ruby Gillis. Each girl writes a story and reads it to the others, and Anne's are the most dramatic.
Mrs Allan reads one of Anne's stories and says that it is very exciting. She suggests, kindly, that Anne should try to write about ordinary things that she knows from her own life.
One day a pedlar comes to the door with a case of goods to sell. Anne sees a bottle of hair dye that promises to turn any hair a beautiful, glossy black.
Anne runs up to her room and locks the door. She puts the dye on her hair with a comb, and she dreams of the lovely black hair she will have.
When Anne looks in the mirror, she screams, because her hair has turned a dull and dreadful green. She cannot believe that such a thing has happened, and she tries to wash it out in vain.
Marilla comes home, sees the green hair, and says that the only cure is to cut it off. Anne cries over her hair, which is as short as a boy's, but she says that she has learned her lesson.
Anne goes back to school with short hair, and the other girls stare. Diana tells her that she looks quite nice, and she says that real friends do not care about hair.

Anne and her friends decide to act out a story about a Lily Maid from a famous poem by Tennyson. Anne will play the lovely Elaine, who floats down the river in a boat, and the others will play her mourners.

Anne lies in the boat with her hands folded, and the others push her away from the shore. She is floating along beautifully when she feels water at her feet, and she sees that the boat is leaking badly.
The boat sinks, and Anne scrambles onto a wooden post under the bridge, where she clings for dear life. Gilbert Blythe happens to come along in his rowing boat, and he rescues her.
On the shore Gilbert asks if they can be friends, and he says that he is sorry for teasing her. Anne thanks him coldly for the rescue, but she says she will never forgive him.
That evening Anne begins to wonder whether she was right to refuse. She feels a small, secret wish that she had said yes, but she is too proud to say so to anyone.
In the spring Anne and Diana walk together in a lane where the trees arch overhead. They share their dreams of the future, and they promise that they will always be friends.
Anne is fourteen now, and she has grown tall and thin. Marilla notices that she talks less than she used to, and she feels a little sad, because she misses the funny little girl.
Miss Stacy forms a special class to prepare the older pupils for the examination to Queen's Academy in Charlottetown. Those who pass can go on to become teachers.
Seven pupils join the class: Anne, Gilbert, Ruby, Jane, Josie Pye, Charlie Sloane and Moody Spurgeon. Diana's parents decide that she will not go, and Anne is sad.
Every evening Anne studies Latin, algebra and geometry by lamplight. She finds geometry the hardest of all, and some nights she wants to throw her book across the room.
In class Anne and Gilbert fight for the top place, and each wants to beat the other. Gilbert is better at some subjects and Anne at others, and they still never speak.
One evening Matthew has a sudden pain in his chest and has to sit down. The doctor tells him that his heart is weak, and that he must avoid heavy work and any shock or worry.
Anne is frightened by the news about Matthew's heart, and she sits beside him in the evening. She tells him that she will work harder than ever, and that she will make him proud.
In June Miss Stacy's pupils travel to Charlottetown to take the examination for Queen's Academy. It is the first time that most of them have been in the city, and they are all very nervous.
In the examination hall Anne works through her papers one by one, and the questions seem hard. When she reaches the geometry paper, she is afraid that she has made terrible mistakes.
Back at Green Gables, Anne waits for the results and cannot sleep. She tells Diana that she is sure that she has failed, and Diana says that she is certain Anne has passed.
One evening Diana races across the fields with a newspaper in her hand. She shouts that the pass list is out, and that Anne has not only passed, but is first, tied with Gilbert.

Matthew and Marilla are very proud, though Marilla hides it behind a stern face. Mrs Lynde and the neighbours come to Green Gables to congratulate Anne, and her friends Jane and Ruby have passed as well.
Anne and the other girls are invited to take part in a concert at the White Sands Hotel. The guests are rich summer visitors, and Anne is told that she is to recite a poem.
On the night of the concert Anne wears a white dress, and she feels shy among the fine ladies in their silks and jewels. Diana and the others stand beside her and hold her hand.
When it is her turn, Anne steps forward, and her fear falls away. She recites so well that the audience sits quite still, and the applause that follows is long and loud.
After the concert, Anne and Diana drive home in the moonlight, talking all the way. Anne says that the hotel was wonderful, but that nothing is as dear to her as Green Gables.
Marilla tells Anne that she and Matthew have decided to send her to Queen's Academy in the autumn. Anne will board in Charlottetown, and she is so happy that she can hardly speak.
Marilla and Mrs Lynde make new dresses for Anne, and her trunk is packed. On her last evening, Anne says goodbye to Diana at the Dryad's Bubble, and both girls cry.
On the morning she leaves, Matthew drives Anne to the station, and he hardly says a word. Marilla stands in the doorway and waves, and for once she does not try to hide her tears.

In Charlottetown Anne finds a room in a boarding house, and she knows nobody except her friends from Avonlea. On the first evening she feels lonely among the crowds of strangers, and she misses Green Gables.
At Queen's Anne hears about the Avery scholarship, which will pay for four years at Redmond College. It is given to the best student in English, and Anne decides at once that she will win it.
At Queen's Anne means to finish two years of work in one winter. She studies until late at night, and she takes only a little time to walk with her friends and to write letters home.
On some weekends Anne goes home by train, and Matthew is always waiting at the station. At Green Gables Marilla cooks all her favourite things, and the old house feels more precious than ever.
At Christmas Anne comes home for the holidays, and the kitchen at Green Gables is full of light and warmth. She tells Matthew and Marilla about her studies, and they listen eagerly to every word.

In the spring Anne takes a walk by the harbour, and she thinks about all that has happened since she first came to Green Gables. She feels that she has grown a great deal and that a new life is beginning.
