In June the final examinations arrive, and Anne writes her papers in a hall full of anxious students. She does her best, and when she comes out, she feels that she has done reasonably well.
Anne says goodbye to the teachers and friends she has made at Queen's. She goes home to wait for the results, and she tries not to think about the medal or the scholarship.
The results are posted on a board at Queen's, and the students crowd around it. Gilbert wins the gold medal, and Anne wins the Avery scholarship, and her friends cheer loudly.
Gilbert hurries over to congratulate Anne on her success, and he seems truly glad for her. She thanks him politely, but she cannot help noticing the warmth in his face.
Anne travels home on the train with her scholarship in her mind. She watches the golden fields go by, and she thinks of Green Gables and all the people who have helped her.
Diana runs down the road to hug Anne as soon as she steps down from the buggy. Mrs Lynde comes to congratulate her, and Marilla cooks a supper of all of Anne's favourite foods.
That evening Matthew sits beside Anne on the porch and says that he is very proud of her. He tells her that he would not trade her for a dozen boys, and that it was a girl who won the scholarship.
Anne takes his hand and tells him that she is glad that he brought her home from Bright River. Matthew smiles his shy smile and says nothing, but he squeezes her hand.
All summer Anne makes plans for her studies at Redmond College. Mrs Allan and the neighbours encourage her, and she dreams of the books she will read and the friends she will make.
Anne and Diana sit by the Dryad's Bubble and talk about the future. Diana is sad that Anne will leave, and they promise to write to each other and to remain friends for ever.
As the summer goes on, Matthew grows more tired. Marilla notices that he is working less and resting more, and she does not like the look of him.
One quiet evening Anne sits by her window in the moonlight and looks at the orchard. She is thankful for everything: for Green Gables, for her friends and for the people who love her.
All of Matthew's savings are kept in the Abbey Bank. Marilla has heard rumours that the bank is in trouble, and she begs him to take his money out, but Matthew trusts the bank.
In the evening Anne sits beside Matthew and tells him about the books she hopes to read at Redmond. He listens to every word with a quiet smile, and he looks happier than he has for weeks.
A few days later Matthew picks up a newspaper at the post office and reads it as he walks home. It says that the Abbey Bank has failed, and that many people have lost their savings.
Matthew comes into the kitchen and tells Marilla that the Abbey Bank has failed. Marilla says that it is a pity, but that nothing can be done, and she tells him to try not to worry.
That evening Anne comes home from Diana's with a bunch of flowers. She sees Matthew standing near the door with a newspaper in his hand, and he looks very grey.
Anne asks Matthew whether he is ill, but he does not answer. He sways, and the paper falls from his hand, and he sinks to the ground as Anne cries out for Marilla.
Marilla and Anne carry Matthew into the house with the help of a neighbour who is passing. Someone runs for the doctor, but it is already too late.
The doctor says that Matthew died at once of heart failure, and that the shock of the news must have caused it. He tells Marilla that the old man felt no pain at all.
Mrs Lynde comes to help, and she takes charge of the house and all that must be done. Anne is too stunned to weep, and she sits silently at the window, looking out at the dark orchard.
In the early morning Anne goes into the garden and picks the little white roses from the old bush that Matthew loved. She lays them beside him, and she gazes at his quiet, kind face.
The whole village comes to Matthew's funeral, and the church is full. Mr Allan speaks about the quiet, gentle man who worked so hard and said so little.
At the graveside the neighbours talk quietly of Matthew's kindness. They say that he was the shyest man in Avonlea, but that he never refused to help anyone who asked.
After the funeral the house is dreadfully quiet, and Anne cannot rest. She wanders from room to room and sees Matthew's chair, his hat on its nail and his boots at the door.
One evening Anne finds herself smiling at the sunset, and then she feels guilty. She thinks it is wrong to be happy when Matthew has gone, and she tells Mrs Allan how she feels.
That night the tears finally come, and Anne cries for a long time into her pillow. She remembers Matthew's shy smile at the station, and she weeps for the kind man who welcomed her.
Marilla comes into the room and sits on the edge of the bed and takes Anne in her arms. She says that she loves Anne as dearly as if she were her own daughter.
Marilla tells Anne that she has never been good at showing her feelings, and that she is sorry for it. She says that Matthew was wiser than she was when he wanted to keep Anne.
Slowly the days pass, and the time for Redmond comes closer. Anne reads her letter from the college, and she begins to wonder whether she can leave Marilla alone.
Marilla tells Anne that Matthew's savings were lost with the bank. She says that the farm is hard to run without him, and that she has little money to spare.
Marilla's headaches have been getting worse, and her sight is failing. At last she decides to go to Charlottetown to see a doctor who specialises in eyes.

The specialist tells Marilla that she must give up reading, sewing and anything else that strains her eyes. He says that if she is careful, her sight may not get worse, but that she may go blind if she is not.
Marilla says that she cannot manage the farm alone with her bad eyes. She thinks that she will have to sell Green Gables, because there is no other way.
That night Anne lies awake for hours and thinks about Marilla and Matthew. She remembers everything that they did for her, and she asks herself what she owes them in return.
In the morning Anne comes downstairs with a calm face, and she tells Marilla that she has made up her mind. She will give up the scholarship, and she will stay at Green Gables.
Marilla says that she cannot let Anne give up her future for an old woman. Anne answers that she will not let Green Gables be sold, and at last Marilla gives way with tears in her eyes.
Anne explains that she will find work as a teacher at a school near home, so that she can live at Green Gables. She will study in her free time, and she says that Marilla will not be alone.
Anne goes to see Mr Barry, who has often wanted more land. He agrees to rent the fields at Green Gables, and Marilla will have a little money coming in.
Anne tells Diana about her decision, and Diana is so glad that Anne is staying that she cries. She says that she was dreading the autumn, and that now it will be the best she has ever had.
Mrs Lynde bustles up the lane and says that the trustees gave the Avonlea school to Gilbert Blythe. She says that Gilbert has given it up so that Anne can have it, and he will teach at White Sands.
Anne is astonished by Gilbert's kindness, and she thinks of how coldly she treated him. She decides to go and find him at once and thank him, and perhaps to put an end to their quarrel.
Anne finds Gilbert walking along the road in the late afternoon. She thanks him for giving up the Avonlea school, and she holds out her hand, which surprises him very much.
Gilbert says that they were meant to be good friends, and that they have been fighting destiny for long enough. Anne laughs, says she is sorry about the long quarrel, and they walk home together.
Marilla has seen them from the window, and she is not displeased. She tells Anne that she once quarrelled with Gilbert's father, and that she has often wished since that she had forgiven him.
In the autumn Anne begins her work as a teacher at the Avonlea school. She is determined to be patient and kind, and she wants every child to love learning.
In the evenings, after her day at school, Anne reads aloud to Marilla by the lamp. Marilla's eyes are resting, and the doctor says that her sight is no worse.
Anne and Diana remain the dearest of friends, and they often walk together after school. They talk about their plans and dreams, and they know that whatever happens, they will stay close.
Anne finds that she loves teaching, and that she is good at it. She remembers how it felt to be a child who was not understood, and she is gentle with every pupil.
One evening Anne goes to Matthew's grave, and she kneels beside it among the white roses. She tells him that she is trying to be a good daughter to Marilla and a good teacher to the children.
Anne walks home from the churchyard in the golden evening, thinking about her life. She remembers the thin, wild child who came on the train, and she knows how much she has to be thankful for.
Anne stops where the road makes a bend, and she cannot see what lies ahead. Yet she is not afraid, because she believes that the road holds good things for her, and she goes on towards home.
C1C2: Mrs Rachel Lynde lives exactly where the main road of Avonlea dips into a leafy hollow, with a small brook running through it, and from her window she can watch the whole village go by. She prides herself on knowing everybody's business, and she always finishes her housework early so that nothing on the road can escape her notice. On this bright afternoon in early June, her knitting lies forgotten in her lap, because something very odd is happening outside.

Down the road comes Matthew Cuthbert in his buggy, wearing a clean white collar and his best suit, while the sorrel mare trots along at a smart and unaccustomed pace. Matthew is the shyest man in Avonlea, who avoids visiting as other men avoid the dentist, and he never leaves the farm on a working afternoon without a very good reason. Mrs Lynde, who cannot bear a mystery, decides at once that she will walk up to Green Gables after tea and discover the truth.

Green Gables stands at the end of a long lane, hidden among orchard trees and set so far back from the road that nobody could call it a neighbourly house. Mrs Lynde walks straight into the spotless kitchen, where Marilla Cuthbert, a tall, thin woman with dark hair streaked with grey, is sitting beside a window full of evening light. In her usual direct way, she asks where Matthew has gone in such fine clothes.

Marilla answers calmly, as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world, that she and Matthew have decided to adopt a boy from the orphan asylum at Hopetown in Nova Scotia. Mrs Spencer, a neighbour from White Sands, has chosen him, and he is due to arrive at Bright River station on the evening train. Matthew has driven eight miles to meet him, and Marilla seems quite untroubled by the news that she has just dropped on her visitor like a stone.

Mrs Lynde is so astonished that for a moment she can say nothing at all, and then she declares that Marilla is taking a fearful risk. Her mind fills with every tale she has ever heard of orphan boys who burned down houses in the night or dropped poison into the well, and she repeats them one by one. She is quite certain, she adds, that nothing good can come of bringing a stranger into a quiet household like this one.

Marilla replies, with the firmness of a woman who has already thought it all through, that Matthew is nearly sixty and no longer as lively as he was. His heart troubles him badly, good hired men are scarce, and the only boys she can find to hire are half-grown and careless and cannot be trusted. A boy from the asylum, she believes, can be taught and trained from the beginning and will grow up to be a comfort to them both.

The sorrel mare carries Matthew eight miles along the red road, past farms and orchards that are pale with blossom and fields that slope away into a haze of pearl and purple. Little birds sing as though this were the one perfect day of the whole summer, and the air is so sweet that even a silent man could be forgiven for smiling. Matthew nods to every traveller he meets, because on the island it is the custom to greet everyone on the road, whether you know them or not.

Matthew has always been afraid of women, with the exception of Marilla and Mrs Lynde, because he cannot shake the feeling that these mysterious creatures are secretly laughing at him. As the buggy rattles along, he hopes that the boy will be a cheerful, sturdy fellow who will chatter happily and expect nothing in the way of conversation. If the child turns out to be shy as well, Matthew thinks, then the long drive home will at least be a peaceful one.

When Matthew reaches Bright River, he sees at once that the evening train has come and gone, and the long platform lies empty in the dusty light. There is no boy anywhere to be seen, and the only living creature in sight is a small girl perched alone on a heap of shingles at the far end. Matthew looks carefully in every other direction, ignores her completely, and goes to ask the stationmaster where on earth the boy has got to.

The stationmaster, who is locking up for the night, tells Matthew that a passenger was put off the train for him, and he nods towards the girl on the shingles. She was offered a seat in the ladies' waiting room, he says with a smile, but she politely refused because she felt there was far more scope for imagination outside. Matthew feels his heart sink to his boots, because it is a boy that he has come for, and nobody has said a word about a girl.

Before Matthew can find a single word, the girl springs up from the shingles and holds out a thin little hand, and her voice is sweet and clear. She tells him that she is delighted to see him, because she was beginning to fear that he had forgotten her, and that she had already made a plan for the night. If he had not come, she says, she would have walked down the track to the big wild cherry tree at the bend, climbed into it, and slept among the blossoms in the moonlight.

Matthew sees a thin child in a very short, very tight dress of yellowish-grey cloth and a faded brown sailor hat, with two braids of thick red hair hanging down her back. Her small white face is covered with freckles, her mouth is wide, and her large eyes look green in one light and grey in the next, as if they change with her feelings. He offers to carry her shabby carpet bag, but she explains that it is not heavy and that the handle needs a special knack, so she had better keep it herself.

Matthew lifts the girl and her bag into the buggy, gathers up the reins, and the sorrel mare sets off along the road toward Avonlea. Anne begins to talk before they have gone a hundred yards, and she pours out her thoughts so quickly that there is no space in which a shy man might put a word. Matthew decides that the unfortunate mistake can wait until Marilla is there to deal with it, since Marilla is far better at such things.

Soon the road enters a long avenue of apple trees, whose branches meet overhead in a tunnel of snowy blossom, and the evening light shines through it like the inside of a pearl. Anne is struck silent for a moment, which for her is a remarkable event, and then she declares that nobody could call such a place by an ordinary name. She decides, with perfect confidence, that it will be known as the White Way of Delight, and Matthew, to his own surprise, finds that the name suits it.

Further along, the road runs beside a broad pond, which lies pink and silver under the sunset, and Matthew remarks that it is called Barry's Pond. Anne cannot bear it, for she feels that a name like that is a poor reward for so much beauty, and she announces that it must be the Lake of Shining Waters. She says she knows she has chosen well because she feels a thrill all the way down her spine, and Matthew, who has never felt one, accepts her word for it.

Anne tells him that someone on the train said the island was the loveliest place in the world, and then she wonders why the roads are such a bright red colour. Matthew confesses that he has never thought about it, and she is not in the least disappointed, because she believes it is a splendid thing that there are so many mysteries still waiting to be solved. The world is such an interesting place, she says, that it makes her glad to be alive.

Anne's voice grows softer as she explains that she has never truly belonged to anybody, and that the thought of going to a real home fills her with joy and a little fear. She hopes that there will be a girl of her own age nearby who will become her bosom friend, someone to whom she can tell her deepest secrets. Matthew, thinking carefully, tells her that there is a girl called Diana Barry living close by, and that she seems a very nice child.

Matthew has not heard so many words in a single evening in all the years of his life, and he feels slightly dizzy from the effort of following them. Yet, to his great surprise, he discovers that he does not mind at all, since the strange child talks with such honesty and cheerfulness that it is rather like listening to a bird. Whatever Marilla may say when they reach home, he thinks, this has been the pleasantest drive he can remember.

By the time the buggy turns into the lane of Green Gables, the dusk has deepened, and a warm lamp is shining in the kitchen window. Marilla comes to the door, looks at the strange small figure beside her brother, and demands to know where the boy is. Matthew, who has been dreading this moment for the last eight miles, gets down slowly from the buggy and says that there was no boy, only this one.

Marilla declares that there must have been a mistake, since it was certainly a boy that they had asked for, and the words fall on the little girl like a blow. Anne drops her bag, clasps her hands, and cries that they do not want her because she is not a boy, and that she ought to have known that it was all too beautiful to last. Then she sits down at the kitchen table, buries her face in her arms, and begins to sob as though her heart would break.

Marilla turns on her brother and asks what on earth he was thinking, and Matthew can only answer, with a helpless look, that he could not leave a child alone at a dark station. The kitchen fills with the sound of Anne's sobbing, and Marilla, who has little practice at comforting anyone, tells her sharply that there is no need to cry so. It is plain, however, that her words have no effect at all, and the two grown people stand there feeling very foolish.

Marilla sets bread and butter and a dish of plum preserves before the child, but Anne only stares at them and cannot swallow a mouthful. When Marilla asks for her name, the girl begs to be called Cordelia, which she thinks the most elegant name in the world, before admitting that she is really Anne Shirley. She adds that she hopes it will at least be spelled with an e, because that looks so much more distinguished on the page.

Marilla takes up a candle and leads the weary child upstairs to the little room under the east gable, where there is a narrow bed, a chair and almost nothing else. Everything is spotlessly clean and painfully bare, and when Marilla has gone downstairs, Anne undresses, climbs into bed and cries into the pillow. Eventually, worn out by the long day and the great disappointment, she sinks into a deep sleep.

In the kitchen below, Marilla tells her brother that there is nothing to be done except to ask Mrs Spencer to take the child back to the asylum. A girl, she says, is of no use on a farm, and she cannot see what the two of them are supposed to do with her. Matthew answers only that she is a nice little thing, that she is so set on staying, and that it does seem a pity to send her away.

Anne wakes to a flood of June sunshine and for a moment cannot remember where she is, until the memory of yesterday's sorrow comes back. Then she runs to the window and pushes it open, and a great cherry tree, white with blossom, brushes the glass as though it had come to say good morning. She decides at once that it must have a name, and she calls it the Snow Queen.

At breakfast, Anne is unusually quiet, and she pushes her plate aside with the air of a tragic heroine. She explains to Marilla that she is in the depths of despair, and she asks whether Marilla herself could eat when feeling so miserable. Marilla, who has never been in the depths of anything, replies drily that she has no idea, and orders her to tell the whole story of her life.

Anne tells her story from the very beginning: she was born in Bolingbroke in Nova Scotia, where her father, Walter Shirley, was a teacher and her mother, Bertha, was his wife. She was only three months old when they both died of a fever within days of each other, and nobody wanted to take the orphan baby. It was the kind neighbour, Mrs Thomas, who finally said that she would take her, and so Anne was brought up by hand.

Anne describes how she worked for Mrs Thomas, helping with four children, until the day her husband was killed by a train and the household broke up. She was then taken in by Mrs Hammond, who had eight children, three pairs of them twins, and whose babies she carried about all day long. When Mr Hammond died, Mrs Hammond sold up and went to live with relatives, and nobody had room for a girl of Anne's age.

After the Hammonds, Anne was sent to the asylum at Hopetown, where she spent four lonely months waiting for someone to choose her. Even before that she had made her own company, imagining that her reflection in a bookcase window was a girl named Katie Maurice, and that the echo she heard in the woods was another called Violetta. She tells Marilla, quite seriously, that she used to tell both of them everything, and that they never once told a secret.

When the story is finished, Marilla sends the girl out to the garden and stands for a moment in thought, looking much less sure of herself than she had hoped. In the yard Matthew, who has been working near the door, says in his slow, shy way that he would rather like to keep the child. Marilla stares at him as though he had suggested keeping a hurricane in the house, but she cannot quite find the words to refuse.

That afternoon Marilla puts Anne in the buggy and drives her to White Sands to ask Mrs Spencer what ought to be done about the mistake. Anne is frightened of what the answer will be, but she makes up her mind not to waste the journey, and she looks eagerly at every tree, field and flower along the way. If she is to be sent back to the asylum, she reasons, she will at least have a few beautiful things to remember.

Mrs Spencer throws up both hands in dismay when she hears that the Cuthberts wanted a boy, for she was quite certain that they had asked for a girl. Somewhere along the way the message must have been muddled, she says, though she cannot imagine how, and she is full of apologies and good will. Anne waits on the porch with her heart in her mouth while the two women discuss what is to become of her.

In the middle of the conversation, Mrs Peter Blewett arrives, a sharp-faced woman who announces that she is looking for a girl to help in her busy house. She examines Anne from head to foot as though she were a horse at a fair, and Anne shrinks back in fear. Marilla, who has heard that Mrs Blewett is a hard mistress who works her helpers to the bone, finds that she likes the woman no better for a closer look.

Marilla looks at the sharp face, then at the trembling child, and finds that she cannot bring herself to leave a girl in the care of such a woman. She tells Mrs Spencer firmly that she will take Anne home again and talk the matter over with Matthew, and that nobody need wait for an answer. It is the first time that she has admitted, even privately, that there might be another way of settling the question than sending the child back.

As the buggy rolls home in the evening light, Marilla says without looking round that she and Matthew have decided to keep Anne, provided that she is good and grateful and tries to learn. For once in her life, Anne has nothing to say, and she sits very still with her hands pressed together, as if she were afraid that the slightest movement might break the spell. When at last she finds her voice, she promises with all her heart to be the best girl on Prince Edward Island.

At bedtime Marilla tells Anne to kneel and say her prayers, and she is horrified to discover that the child has never learned a single one. Anne explains, with perfect honesty, that Mrs Thomas once told her that God had made her hair red on purpose, and that she has never cared much for Him since. Marilla is so shocked that for a moment she cannot answer, and then she decides that this girl must be taught before she is anything else.

Anne kneels and prays in her own words, since nobody has taught her any other, and she begins by thanking God for the White Way of Delight, the Lake of Shining Waters and the Snow Queen. She asks that she may be allowed to stay at Green Gables and that she may be good-looking when she grows up, and she signs herself at the end with her full name, like a letter. Marilla stands in the doorway, torn between horror and the strangest urge to laugh.

Marilla gives Anne a short prayer to learn by heart, and Anne promises eagerly that she will have it perfect by the next evening. Marilla also lays down the rules of the house, which are that Anne must be tidy, helpful and obedient, and must not talk when there is work to be done. Anne agrees to everything with such enthusiasm that Marilla suspects she has not understood how hard the last rule will be.

Marilla sets Anne to sew a patchwork quilt out of small squares of cotton, a task which she considers excellent training for a young girl. Anne bends over her needle with a long sigh and declares that patchwork gives no scope at all for the imagination, since one square is just like the next. Marilla, who never doubts the value of plain work, tells her that she will sew every square, and sew them properly.

For two weeks Mrs Lynde has been kept at home by illness, which has been a torment to a woman so fond of knowing everything, and she has heard about Anne only from other people. As soon as she is well enough, she climbs the lane to Green Gables, determined to see the red-haired orphan with her own eyes and judge for herself. Anne, seeing her coming, looks up from her patchwork with a feeling of dread that she cannot explain.

Mrs Lynde settles herself in the kitchen, folds her hands, and studies Anne from head to foot for so long that the girl begins to turn red. She tells Marilla, in a voice meant to be heard by everybody, that the child was certainly not chosen for her looks. Mrs Lynde has never believed that kindness and plain speaking can be separated, and she is perfectly sure that she is doing Marilla a favour.

Mrs Lynde calls the child terribly skinny and plain, remarks that her freckles are dreadful, and then adds that her hair is as red as carrots. She says all this in a cheerful, conversational tone, as though she were discussing the weather, and she seems quite unaware that she has said anything unkind. Anne stands rigid in the middle of the floor with her hands clenched and her face flaming.

Anne's temper breaks all bounds, and she stamps her foot on the kitchen floor and cries out that she hates Mrs Lynde with all her heart. She asks how anyone would like to be called skinny, plain and freckled to her face, and she says that she does not care if it hurts her feelings. Her voice shakes, her eyes blaze and her whole thin body trembles with rage, while the two women stare at her in silence.

Marilla, white with shock, orders Anne upstairs to her room, and the child runs from the kitchen and slams the door behind her. Mrs Lynde gets up, offended and breathless, and tells Marilla that the child is very badly behaved and that she will have her hands full. Marilla replies as calmly as she can that Anne ought not to have said such things, but that Mrs Lynde ought not to have said what she did.

For two days Anne stays shut up in the little east gable room, lying on her bed and crying until her eyes are red and swollen. Marilla, who believes firmly that a child must learn to say she is sorry, will not let her come down until she agrees to apologise to Mrs Lynde. The trays that she carries upstairs return half full, and Marilla's face grows harder, though her heart is troubled.

Matthew, who cannot bear to hear a child cry, creeps up the stairs on tiptoe, glancing over his shoulder as though he were doing something wicked. He tells Anne in a low voice that she had better do what Marilla wants, since Marilla is a very determined woman and will never give way. He adds, with a clumsy kindness, that it is not so hard to apologise once one has made up one's mind.

Anne decides that if she must apologise, she will do it in the grandest style, and she walks to Mrs Lynde's kitchen and falls on her knees with her hands clasped. She pours out a long and dramatic apology, confessing that she is a wicked and ungrateful girl, who does not deserve any kindness, and that she can never be forgiven. Marilla, standing quietly behind her with her lips pressed tightly together, finds it very hard to keep a straight face.

Mrs Lynde, who cannot hold a grudge against anyone who has humbled herself so thoroughly, tells Anne to get up and admits that she may have been a little too outspoken. She remembers a girl at her own school whose hair was as red as a carrot, which turned in time into a handsome auburn, and she says that Anne's may do the same. Anne walks home in the golden evening, light as a feather, and tells Marilla that it is wonderful to have been forgiven.

On Sunday morning, Anne finds that her plain brown hat is far too dull for a day of such beauty, and she gathers a great armful of buttercups and wild roses to decorate it. She sets the heavy crown of flowers on her head, studies it in the mirror with deep satisfaction, and sets off for church. She is so happy and so sure that everyone will admire it that she walks along with her chin high.

In the church pew, the neighbours stare at the astonishing hat, and some of the girls nudge each other and whisper behind their hymn books. Anne does not notice, because she is lost in the music and the stained light, though she finds the sermon so long that her thoughts wander off across the fields. Marilla, who has just seen the hat in the full light of day, wonders how she can have let the child leave the house in it.

Back at the house, Marilla tells Anne firmly that a hat covered with buttercups and wild roses is quite unsuitable for church, and that the neighbours were laughing at it. Anne is sorry, and she promises to wear her plain hat in future, though she admits that she is rather glad she did not know, since she enjoyed herself so much. Marilla finds that she is not able to be as stern as she meant to be.

One afternoon Marilla gives Anne an errand to Orchard Slope, the Barrys' farm on the far side of the woods, where she is to ask Mrs Barry for the loan of a pattern. Anne walks there through the cool green trees, so full of excited hope and nervous fear that she hardly sees the flowers beside the path. She has been told that the Barrys have a daughter her own age, and she wonders anxiously whether the girl will like her.

In the garden among the willows, Anne finds a pretty girl with black hair, rosy cheeks and merry black eyes, who is gazing at her with great curiosity. This is Diana Barry, the daughter of the house, and she smiles shyly at the strange red-haired girl who has come out of the woods to see her. Anne feels her heart beat faster, for she knows at once that this is the moment she has dreamed about for years.

Anne takes a deep breath and asks Diana, with her hands tightly clasped, whether she thinks she could ever like her enough to be her bosom friend. Diana bursts out laughing, because she has been told that the new girl at Green Gables is a very queer one, and it seems to be true. But her laugh is a friendly one, and she says that she would be glad to have a friend, since there are no other girls near enough to play with.

Anne explains that real friends must swear an oath, and Diana, who has never done such a thing, agrees to try. They stand face to face beside the garden fence and join their hands, and Anne makes up the words as she goes, promising to be faithful to her bosom friend for as long as the sun and moon endure. Diana thinks that it is the loveliest oath she has ever heard, and she says it after her, laughing a little but very much in earnest.

Anne runs home through the woods so lightly that her feet seem scarcely to touch the ground, and she bursts into the kitchen with her face shining. She tells Marilla, without waiting to draw breath, that she has found her bosom friend at last, that her name is Diana, and that she has black hair and a very kind heart. Marilla, who has handed over the pattern with a sigh of relief, can only shake her head and smile.

In the warm weeks that follow, Anne and Diana spend every free hour together in the woods and meadows around Green Gables. Anne cannot let any place go without a name that suits its character, and so the little spring becomes the Dryad's Bubble, while the sunny hollow full of wild flowers is christened Violet Vale. Diana, who has lived near these places all her life and never thought of calling them anything, finds that she can no longer see them in the old way.

Marilla announces that the Sunday school picnic will be held on Wednesday, and that Anne may go with the other children, to the girl's wild delight. She has never been to a picnic in her life, and the thought of games and boat rides and ice cream makes her dizzy with joy, and for days she can talk of nothing else. She tells Marilla that she loves looking forward to things, because even if they do not come true, the looking forward can never be taken away.

On Monday evening Marilla goes upstairs to her room and finds that her amethyst brooch, which she always keeps on her pincushion, is no longer there. It was her mother's, she has worn it to church on Sundays for years, and she values it more than anything else she owns. She is certain that she saw it that afternoon, and the thought of where it can have gone makes her very uneasy.

Marilla questions Anne sharply, and the girl admits that she went into the room and pinned the brooch on to see how it looked, but she says that she put it back at once. Marilla, who knows how much the girl likes to invent stories, does not believe a word of it, and she tells Anne that she will have to stay in her room until she tells the truth. She adds, in a voice that frightens the child, that there will be no picnic for a girl who steals.

Anne longs so much for the picnic that she decides to give Marilla what she seems to want, and she invents a full and dramatic confession. She says that she took the brooch out of curiosity, carried it down to the Lake of Shining Waters, and dropped it in the water, and she describes the way it sank with such feeling that it almost sounds true. She says it in the tone of a girl who is already thinking more about the picnic than about the brooch.

Marilla is horrified, for she had hoped that the girl would say it was all a mistake, and now it seems that she has taken the precious brooch and thrown it away. She says in a cold voice that the picnic is out of the question, and that Anne must stay in her room for the whole day. Anne weeps bitterly, and she cannot understand why her good confession has done her so little good.

On the morning of the picnic, Marilla takes her good black shawl out of the drawer, and there, caught in the fringe, hangs her amethyst brooch. She remembers suddenly that she pinned it there herself on Monday afternoon, and then forgot, and the awful truth falls upon her all at once. Anne had never taken it from the room at all, and the whole of her wild confession was a story that Marilla herself had driven out of her.

Marilla climbs the stairs and asks Anne why she told such a wicked untruth, and Anne explains with perfect simplicity that Marilla had said there would be no picnic unless she confessed. Marilla is silent for a moment, and then she says that she was wrong to press the girl so hard, and that she is very sorry, though lying is lying and Anne must never do it again. Anne forgives her warmly and at once, and Marilla finds that this is harder to bear than being scolded.

Anne is hurried away to the picnic, and she spends an afternoon so perfect that she can scarcely believe it is real. The children play games on the shore, they row about the pond in the boats, and she tastes ice cream for the first time in her life and declares that it is the most delicious thing in the world. When she gets home that night, she tells Marilla that she has had a perfectly splendid time, and then falls asleep in the middle of her sentence.

When September comes, Anne goes to school for the first time in Avonlea, walking along the road under the golden trees with Diana beside her. She is so excited that she can hardly keep still, but she is also a little afraid, for she has never been in a proper school with so many children before. Diana squeezes her hand and promises to sit with her, and tells her what she needs to know about everyone she will meet.

In the schoolroom, Anne notices a tall boy named Gilbert Blythe, whose curly brown hair and roguish hazel eyes belong to a person who enjoys mischief. He is the most popular boy in the school, he is fond of teasing the girls, and he has already made up his mind to find out what the new red-haired girl is like. Anne is trying hard to look at her lessons, and she has no idea that the boy across the aisle is staring at her.

While the teacher is busy at the back of the room, Gilbert reaches across the aisle, lifts one of Anne's long red braids, and whispers the word Carrots in a loud and cheerful voice. The whole class hears it, and a ripple of laughter runs along the benches, for the boy has chosen the one word that Anne can never forgive. She feels the heat rise in her face, and her hand tightens on the slate in front of her.

Anne springs to her feet, her eyes flashing, and brings the slate down upon Gilbert's head with all her strength, so that it cracks clean across. The room falls so silent that the ticking of the clock seems loud, and Gilbert, white with shock, sits with his mouth open and not a word to say. It is, as Diana says afterwards, the most exciting thing that has ever happened in the history of the school.

Mr Phillips, who has been taught to expect trouble only from boys, writes on the blackboard that Anne Shirley has a very bad temper, and he makes her stand in front of the class for the rest of the afternoon. Anne endures it with her head held high and her face burning, and she thinks of nothing but the boy who has shamed her. When school ends, Gilbert tells her in a low voice that he is sorry for making fun of her hair, but she walks straight past him as though he were not there.

When Anne reaches home, she announces to Marilla that she will never set foot in the school again as long as Gilbert Blythe is there. Marilla, who has never in her life met a child with so much determination, is annoyed and does not know whether to scold her or to laugh. She decides to ask Mrs Lynde what a sensible woman would do, since she does not feel sure of her own judgement.

Mrs Lynde, who has forgotten her quarrel with Anne and is rather proud of her own sensible advice, tells Marilla to let the child stay at home until she has cooled off. Anne is soon bored by the long days without lessons or company, and Diana comes over every afternoon to tell her everything that has happened. As the weeks pass, the girl begins to feel that she might be willing to go back, as long as she is never asked to speak to Gilbert.

At last Anne returns to school, and she takes her seat with her chin in the air, behaving as though Gilbert were nothing more than a post in the schoolroom wall. She works so hard at her lessons that she soon stands at the top of the class, and Gilbert, who is as proud as she is, begins to work hard to beat her. Thus begins a rivalry that will last for years, though neither of them would ever admit that the other was a worthy opponent.

One afternoon in the autumn, Marilla drives off to a meeting of the Ladies' Aid Society, and she tells Anne that she may invite Diana to tea while she is away. She explains where Anne will find the fruit cake, the cookies and a bottle of raspberry cordial, and she warns her to take good care of the best china. Anne stands at the gate waving, so excited at the thought of entertaining a guest that she cannot stand still.

Diana arrives in her second-best dress, knocks very properly at the front door, and is received by Anne with all the dignity that a lady of the world could show. The two girls sit in the parlour like grown women, discussing the weather, their gardens and the shocking price of dress cloth, and every few minutes one of them has to cough to hide a giggle. It is a splendid game, and Anne, who loves nothing better than pretending, is completely in her element.

Anne fetches a bottle from the shelf in the sitting-room closet, and she pours a rich red drink into two tall glasses with the care of a trained servant. Diana tastes it, declares it the nicest cordial she has ever drunk, and finishes three large tumblers of it, while neither girl suspects that the bottle is really full of Marilla's currant wine. They go on talking merrily for the rest of the afternoon, quite unaware of the trouble that is already on its way.

After a while Diana begins to feel very strange, and her face grows pale and her words come out in a muddle, and at last she says that she must go home at once. She goes off through the orchard staggering a little, while Anne watches her go with a sinking heart and no idea what has gone wrong. The tea party that had begun so beautifully has become, in a single hour, a most alarming business.

When Diana reaches home, her mother quickly discovers that the girl has been drinking wine, and she is shocked and furious beyond words. She decides that Anne did it on purpose, since she cannot believe that such a thing could be an accident, and she announces that Diana is never to play with that wicked child again. The next day she will not even let Anne explain, and she shuts the door on the sobbing girl.

Marilla looks at the half-empty bottle of currant wine and realises that it was an honest mistake, and she goes straight to Orchard Slope to explain it to Mrs Barry. She returns very annoyed, for Mrs Barry would not listen to a word and still thinks that Anne is a dangerous companion for her daughter. Anne weeps into her pillow that night, quite sure that her life is over.

At the edge of the orchard in the fading light, Anne and Diana meet for the last time, and they say goodbye with many tears. They promise that nothing will ever change their friendship, though from now on they can see each other only at school, and with a swift hug they run back to their separate homes. Anne goes in feeling that she is the loneliest and most misunderstood girl in the world, though she is determined not to give up hope.

A new minister comes to Avonlea, and with him arrives his young wife, a gentle, bright-eyed woman who greets every child as though she were truly glad to see them. Anne, who has been warned that grown-up ladies are never to be trusted, takes one look at Mrs Allan's kind face and loves her without a moment's thought. She declares at supper that she wishes more than anything to grow up exactly like her.

Mrs Allan takes over the girls' Sunday school class, and she makes the lessons so interesting that nobody wants to leave. She invites her pupils to ask whatever questions come into their minds, and Anne is happy to take her at her word, producing so many that the other girls begin to nudge each other. Mrs Allan, however, never shows the slightest impatience, and she answers each one with respect.

One evening in the late winter, Diana races across the fields to Green Gables, breathless and crying, and begs for help. Her little sister Minnie May has croup and is struggling for breath, and her parents are away, with nobody in the house but a frightened hired girl who does not know what to do. Marilla, who has never dealt with croup in her life, can only stand and stare, but Anne is already looking for her coat.

Anne tells Marilla quickly that she knows all about croup, since Mrs Hammond's twins were ill with it again and again, and she hurries through the dark to the Barry house. She finds Minnie May burning with fever and fighting for every breath, with the hired girl wringing her hands beside the bed. It is the one moment when all those long, hard years of looking after other people's babies turn out to be useful.

Anne finds a bottle of ipecac syrup in the cupboard and gives it to the little girl every few minutes, exactly as she remembers doing at Mrs Hammond's. She sends the hired girl for hot water and keeps the fire built up, and through the long hours of the night she never lets go of the child's hand. At no time does she think of herself, or of how tired she is, or of how frightened.

Toward morning, the terrible breathing slowly eases and the child falls into a quiet sleep, and when Dr Spencer arrives at dawn, the danger has passed. He tells the Barrys' hired girl that without the clever girl from Green Gables, the little one would not have lived through the night. Anne walks home across the frosty fields in the pink light, so tired that she scarcely knows where she is, but very proud and happy.

A few days later, Mrs Barry comes to Green Gables, and she takes Anne's hands in hers and thanks her with tears in her eyes. She admits that she was wrong to think that the wine had been given on purpose, and she asks the girl to forgive her for her harsh words. Anne, who has never been able to bear a grudge for long, forgives her at once and from the bottom of her heart.

From that day on, Mrs Barry does not stand in the way of the friendship, and the two girls fly into each other's arms as though they had been parted for years. They spend the whole of the winter together, sliding on the frozen pond, building snow castles and swapping secrets, and Anne is as happy as she has ever been. Her bosom friend, she says, has been given back to her, and it is the best gift of all.

That winter Diana's family invites Anne to go with them to a grand concert in Charlottetown, where they are to spend the night in the house of Diana's rich old aunt, Miss Josephine Barry. The great hall is a blaze of lights and silks, a singer in a beautiful gown sings like a nightingale, and afterwards the girls are taken to eat ice cream in a restaurant. Anne tells herself that it is more wonderful than anything she has ever imagined.

That night, the two excited girls undress in the dark and race for the spare bed, leaping into it with a great bounce, only to land on top of somebody. Aunt Josephine, who had gone to bed there without telling them, wakes up with a shout of fright and fury, and the girls run out of the room, shaking with fear and laughter. In the morning she is so angry that she will hardly speak to them, and the whole visit ends in disgrace.

Anne makes a sincere and handsome apology to Miss Barry, who accepts it stiffly, though she cannot quite hide that she is amused, and the girls are sent home. Anne throws her arms around Marilla and says that coming home to Green Gables is the best part of any journey. Marilla, who never says such things aloud, admits gruffly that she is glad, and that the house has been very quiet.

Near the Barry farm there is a dark grove of spruce trees, and Anne and Diana decide to call it the Haunted Wood, because it looks as though it ought to be haunted. They make up a tale about a ghost in white who walks there at night, and every evening they add some new, hair-raising detail, until each of them half believes it is true. Anne, who has the stronger imagination of the two, is the first to be truly frightened and the last to admit it.

One evening at dusk, the two girls are walking beside the dark trees when they begin to imagine that the ghost is really there, and a sudden cold terror seizes them both. They run screaming through the twilight, tripping over roots and stones, and burst into the kitchen at Green Gables as white as sheets. Marilla, who has been waiting with the supper, looks at them in astonishment and then in growing anger.

Marilla tells Anne sternly that her imagination has gone too far and that she will not have any more of this ghost nonsense in her kitchen. She says that Anne has frightened Diana half to death, and that the stories must be forbidden from this moment on. Anne protests that the ghost seemed so real that she could not help it, but Marilla has already made up her mind.

To cure her of her fancies, Marilla sends Anne alone through the Haunted Wood at dusk with a message for the Barrys, and she will listen to no pleading. Anne trembles from head to foot as she goes, imagining a pale shape behind every trunk, but she sees nothing at all, and she runs home again with a thumping heart. She says afterwards that she has learned a lesson, and she never spoils her own peace with ghosts again.

The minister and his wife are to come to tea at Green Gables, and Anne is so thrilled that she cannot sleep. She begs Marilla to let her bake a layer cake for the occasion, because she wants everything to be perfect for the lady she loves best. Marilla, who knows that Anne can be careless, finally agrees, though she says that she will check the cake herself before it goes to the table.

Anne mixes the cake with the greatest care, and it rises in the oven until it is high and golden and beautiful to see. But when she adds the flavouring, she reaches for the wrong bottle on the shelf, one that holds anodyne liniment for sore muscles, and she pours it into the cake in the belief that it is vanilla. She admires the finished cake with great pride, and nothing tells her that the worst is still to come.

At the tea table, Anne watches with shining eyes as Mrs Allan lifts a forkful of the golden cake to her lips, and she sees the lady's face change in the strangest way. Mrs Allan keeps on eating politely, but Anne takes a bite of her own piece, and the horrible taste of liniment fills her mouth. She cries out in horror that the cake is ruined, and Marilla, who has forgotten to inspect it, sits red-faced with embarrassment.

Mrs Allan puts her arm around the sobbing girl and tells her, with perfect kindness, that it was an honest mistake and that anyone might have done the same. She says that the thought behind the cake means more to her than any taste, and she asks Anne to show her the garden after tea, so that the afternoon is saved from disaster. Anne dries her tears and, in the warm sunshine of Mrs Allan's kindness, decides that she loves her more than ever.

One autumn afternoon, Anne and her friends are playing in the Barry garden when Josie Pye, who dislikes her, dares her to walk along the very top of the kitchen roof. Anne, who has never refused a dare in her life and cannot bear to hear Josie sneer, accepts the challenge although her heart sinks. Diana protests in terror, and Ruby Gillis begins to cry, but Anne has already made up her mind.

Anne climbs up the ladder, steps out on the narrow ridge of the roof, and gets about halfway across before she begins to sway. She tries to keep her balance and cannot, and with a cry she slides down the slope and crashes on the ground below, while her friends scream in terror. For a moment the garden is perfectly silent, and then Diana rushes forward with her hands to her mouth.

Anne is carried home in great pain, and the doctor says that her ankle is badly hurt and that she must stay in bed for many weeks. Diana comes every day with the news from school, Mrs Allan visits with books and flowers, and Marilla scolds her in such a tender voice that the words hardly matter. Lying there, Anne decides that she has had her fill of dares, and that she will never again let Josie Pye decide what she shall do.

By the time Anne's ankle has healed and she is able to go back to school, Mr Phillips has gone, and a young woman named Miss Stacy has taken his place. She is clever, bright and full of life, and she treats her pupils as though they were interesting people, which is exactly what they have been longing for. Anne decides within the first week that she would follow Miss Stacy to the ends of the earth.

Miss Stacy has ideas that Avonlea has never heard before, and one of them is that children can learn a great deal outside the school walls. She takes her pupils on long walks in the woods to study birds, flowers and trees, and she asks them to write their own compositions about what they have seen. Anne finds that she has a gift for words, and her essays quickly become the pride of the school.

Before Christmas, Miss Stacy proposes a concert to raise money for a school flag, and all the pupils plunge into rehearsals with enormous excitement. Anne is given a poem to recite, and she practises it in the orchard, in the barn and even in the kitchen, until Marilla declares that she knows the words herself. The night before the concert, Anne is so nervous that she cannot touch her supper.

On the night of the concert the hall is packed, and Anne, standing on the platform in front of so many faces, feels her knees tremble beneath her. But once she begins to recite, the fear drops away, and her clear voice fills the room until the audience sits perfectly still. When she finishes, there is a pause, and then the whole hall bursts into applause, and Matthew, who is sitting at the back, wipes his eyes with a big handkerchief.

Anne has noticed that nearly every girl at school has a new dress with puffed sleeves, and she longs for one more than for anything else in the world. She begs Marilla for a dress like theirs, saying that she would not be so vain if she had it, but Marilla replies firmly that such a fashion is foolish and wasteful. Anne says no more, but she cannot hide her disappointment, and Matthew sees it.

Matthew, who has noticed Anne's sad face, resolves in secret to buy her the dress that she wants, and he goes to a shop in Carmody with great determination. But when he sees the pretty young woman behind the counter, his courage fails entirely, and he buys several things that he does not need before he can bring himself to ask for what he came for. At last he leaves with a length of soft brown cloth under his arm, feeling that he has won a battle.

Matthew knows that he cannot make a dress himself, so he carries the cloth to Mrs Lynde, who is a famous dressmaker, and asks her to make it up. She agrees at once, since she has a soft spot for the strange little girl, and she promises to say nothing to Anne and to put in the very puffed sleeves that the girl wants. For days the dress is made in secret, and Matthew goes about the farm looking like a man with the biggest secret in the world.

On Christmas morning Anne finds a parcel on the kitchen table, and when she opens it, there lies a soft brown dress with the biggest puffed sleeves that she has ever seen. For once in her life she has no words, and she can only hold the dress against her cheek while tears roll down her face. Then she throws her arms around Matthew and tells him that no one has ever been given such a lovely present, and the old man blushes to the roots of his hair.

Anne is never happy without a new scheme, and she starts a story club with Diana, Jane Andrews and Ruby Gillis. The four girls write a story in turn, meet under the apple trees to read it aloud, and admire each other's efforts with great seriousness. Anne's tales are the most dramatic of all, full of beautiful heroines, noble deaths and tragic partings, and the others listen with their mouths open.

Mrs Allan reads one of Anne's stories, and she says that it is full of life and feeling, though perhaps a little too many people are dying in it. With great tact she suggests that Anne might try writing about the world she knows from her own experience, because ordinary people can be every bit as fascinating as imaginary ones. Anne considers this advice solemnly, since anything that comes from Mrs Allan deserves her most careful reflection.

One afternoon a pedlar comes to the kitchen door with a case of small wares, and he tells Anne that he has a bottle that will turn any hair a beautiful, glossy black. Anne, who has hated her red hair for as long as she can remember, can hardly believe her luck, and she buys the bottle for her pocket money at once. Marilla is away at a neighbour's for the afternoon, and nobody is there to stop her.

Anne runs up to her room, locks the door, and pours a little of the dye on her comb, and then she brushes it carefully through every strand of her hair. She imagines how she will look when it is done, with black hair like a princess in a storybook, and she does not spare a thought for what Marilla will say. She puts the bottle down with a happy sigh and goes to the mirror.

When Anne looks into the mirror, a shriek escapes her, for her hair, instead of turning glossy black, has become a dull and dreadful green. She scrubs it again and again with soap and water, but the colour stays as bright as ever, and she realises that she has made the worst mistake of her life. For several days she hides in her room in shame, and the whole village hears of it.

Marilla takes up her scissors, and with a firm hand she cuts off all of Anne's long hair until it is as short as a boy's. Anne cries when she sees herself in the mirror, and then she says in a small voice that she has learned her lesson and will never be vain about her looks again. She also says that she will try, for the rest of her life, never to look in a mirror if she can possibly help it.

Anne goes back to school with her short hair, and the children stare at her as though she had come from another country. Josie Pye makes a cruel remark, but Diana tells her at once that she looks very nice, and that no real friend would care about hair. Slowly the first shock passes, and the days pass, and the hair begins to grow, and Anne begins to see that being laughed at is not the end of the world.

Inspired by a poem by Tennyson, Anne and her friends decide to act out the tragic story of Elaine, the Lily Maid who floats down the river to the castle. Anne will play Elaine, of course, because she can look the most tragic, and the others will be the king, the queen and the mourners. They choose a flat old boat, drape it with a black cloth, and carry it down to the pond in a state of solemn excitement.

Anne lies in the boat with her hands folded on her breast and a lily between them, and the others push her gently out into the stream. For a few lovely minutes she floats along like a real tragic heroine, until she feels water around her ankles and sees to her horror that the boat is leaking badly. The poor old boat is sinking fast, and the nearest bridge is coming towards her with alarming speed.

The boat settles beneath her just as she passes the bridge, and Anne scrambles onto one of the wooden posts, where she clings with all her strength and prays for help. At that moment Gilbert Blythe happens to row past in his small boat, and he sees her at once, and he takes her aboard without a moment's hesitation. He does not laugh at her, though she is dripping and miserable, and he does not say a word until they reach the shore.

When the boat reaches the shore, Gilbert holds out his hand and asks, with real feeling, whether they might not be friends from now on, and he says that he is sorry for teasing her about her hair. Anne pulls her hand away, thanks him in a freezing voice for rescuing her, and declares that she will never forgive him. She marches up the bank with her wet skirts dripping, and she does not once look back.

That evening, when the excitement has died down, Anne sits alone by her window and begins to wonder whether she was right to refuse the boy's hand. A small, secret voice tells her that she might have been kinder, and that she would have felt better if she had been, but she is far too proud to listen to it. She tells herself firmly that Gilbert Blythe is nothing to her and goes to bed.

As spring turns to summer, Anne and Diana spend many long evenings walking in a quiet lane where the branches arch overhead like the roof of a church. They tell each other all their dreams about the future, such as the houses they will live in, the people they will marry and the places they will see. Neither of them can quite imagine that anything in the wide world will ever come between them, and so they walk on, laughing.

By the time she is fourteen, Anne has shot up in height and become a tall, slender girl, with a more serious face and a quieter manner. Marilla notices that she talks less than she did, and that her eyes are often turned toward distant things, and to her own surprise she feels a pang of loss. She almost misses the odd little chatterbox that once arrived at Green Gables, though she would never say so aloud.

Miss Stacy announces that she will form a special class after school to prepare the older pupils for the entrance examination to Queen's Academy in Charlottetown. Those who pass the examination and complete the course there may become teachers, and for the first time many of the farm children begin to see a future beyond the village. Anne's heart leaps within her, for she has secretly longed for just such a chance ever since she first opened a book.

Seven pupils join the Queen's class: Anne, Gilbert, Ruby Gillis, Jane Andrews, Josie Pye, Charlie Sloane and Moody Spurgeon MacPherson. Diana's parents have decided that she does not need so much learning, and Anne feels the separation keenly, because it is the first time that she has had to walk the path of her studies alone. But Diana promises that she will help in any way she can, and for the moment that is a comfort.

Every evening after supper, Anne spreads her books across the kitchen table and works at Latin, algebra, geometry and English literature until her eyes are tired and her head aches. She loves the poetry and finds the Latin interesting, but geometry is another matter, and there are nights when she wants to throw the book across the room. She sticks to it with grim determination, because she means to prove that she can do anything that Gilbert Blythe can do.

In the Queen's class, Anne and Gilbert fight for first place with grim determination, and the whole school watches to see which of them will win. Gilbert is better at Latin and mathematics, Anne is better at composition, and the lead changes from one week to the next, though they never exchange a single word. Anne tells herself that she wants to win only for the glory, but she cannot quite believe it.

One summer evening Matthew comes in from the field, white-faced and breathless, and has to sit down on the nearest chair, because of a sudden pain in his chest. The doctor is sent for, and after examining him he says gravely that the old man's heart is far from sound, and that he must avoid heavy work and, above all, any kind of shock or worry. Matthew accepts the news without complaint, though Anne and Marilla begin to watch him very carefully.

Anne is frightened by the doctor's words, and that evening she sits beside Matthew's chair in the lamplight and takes his hand. She promises him that she will work harder than ever at her lessons, so that all his kindness will be repaid, and that he will never be sorry for having kept her at Green Gables. Matthew looks at her with his shy, gentle smile and says that he is proud of her already.

In June the whole Queen's class travels by train to Charlottetown to sit the entrance examination, and for most of them it is the first time they have seen a city. The streets are loud and crowded, the buildings are tall and strange, and the children from Avonlea cling together like a flock of nervous sheep. Anne, who is more afraid of the examination than she would ever admit, walks beside Jane and Ruby in an anxious silence.

In the large quiet hall, Anne works her way through the papers one by one, and her pen races across the page while the clock ticks in the silence. Most of the questions are fair, but when she reaches geometry, she is almost certain that she has made some terrible mistakes. She comes out at the end of the day pale and weary, convinced that she has failed.

Back at Green Gables, Anne can think of nothing but the results, and she sleeps badly and eats little, and every sound makes her jump. She tells Diana on the porch one evening that she is absolutely sure she has failed, and that she will never be able to look anyone in the face again. Diana, who has more faith in her than she has in herself, laughs and says that she has never heard such nonsense.

One evening Diana comes flying across the fields with a newspaper over her head, so out of breath that she cannot speak at first. When she finds her voice, she cries that the pass list has been printed, and that Anne has not only passed but has come out first of all the island, tied with Gilbert Blythe. Anne reads the names three times with trembling hands before she can believe that it is true.

Matthew's face is full of quiet pride, and even Marilla, who is not a woman to show her feelings, cannot hide a gleam of satisfaction in her eyes. Mrs Lynde and half the neighbours come over to Green Gables that evening to offer their congratulations, and they are glad to hear that Jane Andrews and Ruby Gillis have passed too. Anne goes to bed in a daze of happiness, feeling that her whole life has been a preparation for this one day.

That summer, the girls of Avonlea are invited to take part in a concert at the White Sands Hotel, where rich summer visitors come each year to enjoy the sea air. Anne is asked to recite a poem, and she accepts with a mixture of pride and terror, for she has never stood in front of such fashionable people. For weeks she practises in the garden and the orchard until the hens know the poem by heart.

On the night of the concert, Anne puts on a simple white dress and drives with her friends to the great hotel on the shore, where the long rooms are bright with lamps. The ladies in silks and jewels seem so fine and so distant that she feels like a little country mouse, and her heart sinks. Diana squeezes her hand and tells her that she is the best reciter in Prince Edward Island.

When her turn comes, Anne walks onto the stage with her back straight, and all at once her nervousness vanishes, and the poem seems to speak through her. She recites so beautifully that the great room is perfectly still, and when she finishes there is a long hush and then a roar of applause. A lady in a pink silk dress leans forward and asks her neighbour who the red-haired girl is.

After the concert, the girls drive home through the warm night under a sky full of stars, talking and laughing all the way. Anne says that the hotel was splendid, but that she would not change one small corner of Green Gables for all its marble and silk. Diana says that she always knew Anne was bound for great things, and Anne shakes her head and says she is only bound for home.

A few days later, Marilla tells Anne in her brisk way that she and Matthew have talked it over, and they have decided to send her to Queen's Academy in the autumn. She will board in Charlottetown for the winter, and the money will somehow be found, because they believe that she deserves the chance. Anne, who has hoped for it but never dared to expect it, covers her face with her hands and cannot say a word.

All through August, Marilla and Mrs Lynde sew new dresses for Anne's winter, and a trunk is packed with everything she could possibly need. On her last evening at Green Gables, Anne walks down to the Dryad's Bubble to say goodbye to Diana, and the two girls cry in each other's arms and swear that nothing will ever change. It is the first time that the world has seemed too large for the two of them.

On the morning of her departure, Matthew drives Anne to the station in the old buggy, and for most of the way he says nothing, because there is too much to say. Marilla stands in the doorway of Green Gables and waves until the buggy is out of sight, and for once in her life she does not try to hide her tears. Anne looks back until the lane and the apple trees have vanished behind the hill.

In Charlottetown Anne finds her room in a crowded boarding house, and she realises that, apart from her old friends from Avonlea, she knows nobody in the whole city. The streets are noisy, the faces are unfamiliar, and on the first evening the loneliness comes over her like a wave, so that she almost wishes that she had never come. She sits at the window in the dusk, longing for the white apple blossom and the Lake of Shining Waters.

At the Academy, Anne hears about the Avery scholarship, a great prize that pays for four years at Redmond College, and which is awarded to the best student in English. Gilbert, it is said, is aiming for the gold medal, and Anne feels a new, fierce ambition awaken in her breast. She has always been good at English, and she resolves that this time nobody is going to stop her.

Anne has made up her mind to finish the work of two years in a single winter, and she studies late into the night, long after the boarding house has fallen silent. She allows herself only a few hours a week for walks with her friends and for her long, loving letters to Marilla. Gilbert is working just as hard, and each of them knows that the other is somewhere in the same city, burning a lamp until midnight.

When she can spare the time, Anne goes home to Green Gables for the weekend, and Matthew is always waiting for her at the station with the buggy. Marilla cooks all her favourite foods, and the little east gable room looks more precious to her every time she sees it. She sits by the kitchen window on Sunday evening and drinks in every detail, and she goes back to the city with a lighter heart.

At Christmas Anne comes home for the holidays, and the kitchen at Green Gables is full of warmth and the smell of baking. She tells Matthew and Marilla all about her studies, her teachers and her friends in the boarding house, and they listen to every word as if she were a traveller returned from a far country. Matthew sits quietly in his chair, and it seems to Anne that he looks a little older than he did in the autumn.

In the spring, Anne takes a long walk beside the harbour in Charlottetown, with the wind blowing off the sea, and she thinks of all that has happened since she first came to Green Gables. She feels that she has grown from a wild little girl into a young woman who has ambitions and responsibilities. The future lies before her like a road that has not yet been walked, and she is eager to set out along it.

In June the final examinations arrive, and Anne writes her papers in a silent hall full of pale, anxious students, with the same grim concentration that she has brought to every lesson. She works through each question carefully, and when she comes out at the end, she feels, for the first time in months, that she has done as well as she possibly could. All that remains is to wait for the news, and to find some way of filling the empty hours until it comes.

Anne says goodbye to the teachers and the friends she has made at Queen's, and it surprises her how much she has grown to love the old building and its quiet rooms. She goes home to Green Gables to wait for the results, trying not to think about the medal or the scholarship or the boy who may have beaten her. The long June days pass slowly, and every time she hears a step on the road, her heart leaps.

The results are posted on the notice board at Queen's, and the students surge forward and jostle for a place, crying out the names as they find them. Gilbert Blythe has won the gold medal, and Anne Shirley, to her own astonishment, has won the Avery scholarship, which will pay for four years at Redmond. Her friends cheer so loudly and so long that the whole old building seems to shake, and Anne, who has gone quite pale, can only stand and stare at the board.

In the middle of the noise, Gilbert makes his way to Anne's side and warmly congratulates her on her success, and she can see that he is truly glad for her. She thanks him politely and no more, for old habits die hard, though she cannot help noticing the warmth in his eyes. She is surprised to find that the rivalry that has lasted for so long no longer feels as bitter as it did.

Anne sits at the window of the train as it carries her home through the golden fields of summer, with the scholarship ringing like a bell in her mind. She thinks of Green Gables and of all the people who have helped her on the way, and she knows that she could never have come so far without them. Her heart is so full of gratitude and happiness that she can scarcely keep from laughing aloud in front of the other passengers.

As soon as Anne steps down from the buggy at Green Gables, Diana runs down the road and flings both arms around her, laughing and crying at the same time. Mrs Lynde arrives to offer her congratulations, in her blunt way, and Marilla has prepared a supper of all of Anne's favourite dishes. It is the sort of homecoming that she has dreamed of since the first moment she left.

That evening Matthew sits beside Anne on the porch, with his hands folded and his old hat tilted back, and tells her in his shy, slow way that he is more proud of her than he can say. He says that he would not exchange her for a dozen boys, no, not for a dozen boys all together, and that it was not a boy who won the scholarship but a girl, his own girl. Anne cannot speak, because her throat is too tight, and she can only lean her head against his shoulder in the warm and fading light.

Anne takes Matthew's old, rough hand in both of hers and tells him that she is glad he brought her home from Bright River on that spring evening so long ago. She says that it was the best mistake that anyone ever made, and that she has never regretted it for a single moment. Matthew only smiles his shy smile and squeezes her fingers, but she knows that he has understood every word.

All through the summer, Anne makes plans for her future studies at Redmond College, and she spends long hours dreaming of the books she will read and the friends she will make. Mrs Allan and the other neighbours encourage her warmly, and even Mrs Lynde admits that she may turn out to be a credit to Avonlea after all. The days are full of sunshine, and it seems to Anne that nothing could ever spoil her happiness.

Anne and Diana sit side by side at the Dryad's Bubble, where they have shared so many secrets, and talk quietly about the future. Diana confesses that she is sad that Anne will be going away, and that she does not know what she will do when the long evenings come, but Anne promises to write every week. Neither of them says it aloud, but both feel that their childhood is ending, and that something precious is slipping quietly by.

As the summer goes by, Matthew grows more tired, and Marilla notices that he works much less than he used to, and that he rests more often in the middle of the day. She says nothing to Anne, because she does not want to spoil her happiness, but she lies awake at night and listens to every sound in the house. The old man himself never complains, and whenever she asks how he feels, he insists that he is perfectly well and only a little tired.

On a quiet evening toward the end of summer, Anne sits at the east gable window in the moonlight, looking out at the dark orchard and the shining sky above it. She thinks of all that she has been given, the home, the friends, the learning and the love, and she thanks God with her whole heart for each of them. She does not know that this peaceful evening is the last she will spend with such perfect happiness.

All of Matthew's life savings are in the Abbey Bank, a small institution that a trusted neighbour has recommended to him. Marilla has heard some uneasy rumours about it, and she begs her brother to take out his money before it is too late. Matthew, who has never doubted anyone in his life, answers mildly that he is sure the bank is quite sound.

That evening Anne sits beside Matthew on the porch and tells him about the books she hopes to read at Redmond, and the friends she hopes to make there. The old man listens to every word with a quiet smile, and he looks happier than he has done for weeks, as though her good fortune were a sunlit window into which he could look. When she stops for breath, he only says that he is glad he has lived to see it.

A few days later Matthew picks up a newspaper at the post office, and he begins to read it as he walks slowly home along the road. A short report on the front page announces that the Abbey Bank has failed, and that many of its depositors have lost nearly everything. He reads the news twice, and his face changes in a way that nobody sees.

Matthew comes into the kitchen, sits down heavily by the table and tells his sister in a low voice that the Abbey Bank has failed. Marilla, who suspected that something like this might happen, says that it is a great pity but that nothing can now be done, and she begs him not to dwell on it. She does not realise, as she turns back to her knitting, how deeply her brother has taken the news.

That evening Anne comes home from Diana's through the soft dusk with her arms full of flowers, singing as she walks. At the door of Green Gables she sees Matthew standing with a newspaper in his hand, and in the fading light his face looks strangely grey and still. She stops singing in the middle of a word, and a sudden cold fear closes around her heart like a hand.

Anne asks Matthew whether he is ill and takes a step toward him, but he does not answer, and the newspaper slips from his fingers. He sways for a moment and then sinks quietly to the ground, and Anne drops her flowers and cries out for Marilla in a voice she hardly recognises as her own. Marilla comes running from the kitchen, wiping her hands on her apron, and her face is already as white as the flowers on the ground.

Marilla and Anne carry Matthew into the house, helped by a hired man who happens to be passing, and they lay him on the sofa in the sitting room. Someone runs at full speed to fetch the doctor, and the two women wait in dreadful silence, but they know in their hearts that nothing can now be done. When the doctor arrives, he takes one look at Matthew's face and shakes his head.

The doctor tells them gently that Matthew has died at once of heart failure, brought on by the shock of the bad news, and that he felt no pain at all. It is some comfort to Marilla, who stands rigid and silent by the sofa, though it is a very small one. Anne hears it all as if from a great distance, and she cannot yet feel that it is real.

Mrs Lynde arrives within the hour, and without a word of fuss she takes charge of the house and of all the sad duties that follow a death. Anne sits at the kitchen window, looking out at the dark orchard, and cannot weep, because the loss seems too large to be felt at all.
