Neighbours begin to arrive with food and flowers, speaking in low voices and moving about the house on tiptoe.

In the early morning light, Anne goes out into the garden and picks the little white roses from the old bush that Matthew had always loved, because his mother brought it long ago from Scotland. She carries them in and lays them beside him, and she looks for a long time at his face, which is gentle and peaceful and a little younger than before. She feels that he is only sleeping, and that if she were quiet enough he might wake and smile at her.

On the day of the funeral, the whole village follows the plain coffin down the lane, and the little church is so full that people stand along the walls. Mr Allan speaks warmly about the quiet, gentle man who worked all his life and asked for so little, and many of the farmers wipe their eyes. Anne sits very straight beside Marilla, and she hears the words as though they came from the bottom of a well.

In the churchyard, the neighbours stand with their heads bowed, and one by one they speak of Matthew's kindness in low and respectful voices. They remember that he was the shyest man in Avonlea, who ran away from a conversation as other men run from a fire, but who never refused to help anyone who asked. Marilla listens with her lips pressed tightly together, and a single tear runs down her cheek.

When the funeral is over and the neighbours have gone home, the house seems dreadfully quiet, and Anne wanders from room to room without knowing what she is looking for. She sees Matthew's chair by the kitchen window, his old hat on its nail and his boots standing neatly by the door, and each small object feels like a knife in her heart. She cannot bring herself to move any of them, and she decides with fierce tenderness that nothing shall be touched.

One evening, quite without meaning to, Anne catches herself smiling at the beauty of a sunset, and immediately a wave of guilt overwhelms her. She tells Mrs Allan that it seems wrong to enjoy anything when Matthew is gone, and the minister's wife answers gently that he would be the last person to want her to be sad. Grief, she says, will lessen in its own time, and it will be a sign of love and not of forgetting.

That night the tears finally come, in a great flood that she cannot stop, and Anne cries into her pillow until she has no strength left. She remembers Matthew's shy smile at the station on that spring evening so long ago, and the long drive under the apple blossoms, and every kind thing that he ever did. It is the first time since the funeral that she has felt that she can breathe.

In the darkness the door opens softly, and Marilla comes in and sits on the edge of the bed, and without a word she gathers the weeping girl into her arms. In a voice that is not quite steady, she says that she loves Anne as dearly as her own flesh and blood, and that Anne has been her joy and comfort since the day she arrived. It is the first time that Marilla has ever said such a thing aloud.

Later, Marilla admits to Anne that she has never been good at showing her feelings, and that she is sorry that she has not said these things sooner. She says that when Anne first arrived, she was a stiff and foolish woman who wanted to send her back, and that Matthew was far wiser than she. Anne squeezes her hand and tells her that it does not matter now, because she has always known.

Slowly the days pass, and the date when she must leave for Redmond comes closer, and Anne reads the college's letter again and again. She knows that this is the moment that she has worked toward for so many years, but she cannot picture leaving Marilla alone in the big silent house. The thought sits in her mind all day, and she lies awake at night turning it over.

Marilla sits down with Anne one evening and explains plainly that all of Matthew's savings were lost when the bank failed, and that she has very little money to spare. The farm is a good one, but it needs a strong man to work it, and a woman alone cannot manage it without help. She says it without self-pity, just as she says everything, but Anne can see how heavily it weighs on her.

All this time Marilla's headaches have been growing worse, and her eyesight, which was never very strong, is beginning to fail her badly. Anne has noticed that she holds her sewing close to her face and that she often puts her hand over her eyes, and at last she persuades her to go to Charlottetown to see a specialist. Marilla goes with great reluctance, and she comes back very pale and very quiet.

Marilla returns from Charlottetown pale and quiet, and that evening she tells Anne calmly what the specialist has said. If she gives up reading, sewing and every other task that strains her eyes, and if she can avoid crying, he believes that her sight will not get worse, and her headaches may go. If she does not, she may go blind in the end, and she says it as simply as if she were reading out a recipe.

Marilla looks slowly round the kitchen where she has lived all her life and says that she does not see how she can manage the farm alone with her failing eyes. Hired men are expensive and unreliable, there is no money to spare, and she thinks that the only sensible course is to sell Green Gables and find a small place to live. She says it with a calm face, but Anne sees that her hands are trembling.

That night Anne cannot sleep, and she sits at the east gable window in the moonlight, thinking over everything that has happened. She remembers the lonely little orphan who came to Green Gables, the kindness of Matthew and the patient strictness of Marilla, and she asks herself honestly what she owes them in return. As the stars wheel slowly past the cherry tree, the answer begins to take shape in her mind, plain and clear.

In the morning Anne comes down with a calm, bright face, and she tells Marilla before breakfast that she has made up her mind. She will not go to Redmond, she says, because she cannot leave Marilla alone, and the scholarship will have to be given up. She adds that she has thought about it carefully all night, and that she is quite certain she is doing the right thing.

Marilla protests with all her strength that she cannot let a girl of Anne's gifts throw away her future for the sake of an old woman with bad eyes. Anne answers that it is not a sacrifice, since she loves Green Gables with all her heart and refuses to see it sold, and she will study at home in the evenings. At last Marilla gives way, and for the first time in many years, she weeps openly and does not try to hide it.

Anne explains her plan to Marilla beside the kitchen fire: she will seek a post as a teacher in a school close enough to Green Gables that she can live at home. She will pursue her studies in the evenings, and perhaps return to the university in later years, while Marilla will never be left alone in the house. It is not Redmond, she says, but it is an honourable beginning, and she is confident that she will enjoy it.

Anne goes to see Mr Barry, who has often said that he would like more land, and she asks him whether he would care to rent the fields of Green Gables. He agrees at once, and offers a fair price, so that Marilla will have a little money coming in every year while Anne goes out to teach. Anne walks back across the meadow with the feeling that a great weight has been lifted from her shoulders.

Anne tells Diana the news, and her friend is so glad that Anne is not going away that she bursts into happy tears and flings her arms around her neck. She admits that she has been dreading the autumn, and that now it will be the best that she has ever known, with Anne at home and school to teach. Neither of them can speak for a moment, because their friendship has been tested and has come out stronger.

Mrs Lynde bustles up the lane with the air of a woman who has the best news in the county, and she announces that the trustees have given the Avonlea school to Gilbert Blythe. But, she says, Gilbert has given it up, because he heard that Anne meant to teach at Carmody, and he wanted her to have the school near her home. He will teach at White Sands instead, and she thinks it is very handsome of him.

Anne stands quite still in the lane for several minutes after Mrs Lynde has gone, remembering all the cold words and proud looks with which she has met his kindness over the years. She thinks of the boy in the rowing boat, and the hand he held out on the shore, and she feels more ashamed than she has ever felt. She resolves that she will go and find him at once and thank him, and that she will make an end of their foolish quarrel.

Anne finds Gilbert walking along the road in the golden light of the late afternoon, and she stops in front of him, rather out of breath. She thanks him for giving up the Avonlea school, and then she holds out her hand, which astonishes him so much that for a moment he cannot speak. He takes it and holds it a little longer than is strictly needed, his eyes shining.

Gilbert tells her that they were born to be good friends, and that they have been thwarting destiny quite long enough. Anne laughs, and says that she is sorry for the stubborn, silly quarrel and that she has wanted to forgive him ever since the day of the boat, though she never knew how to say it. They walk together along the lane in the red-gold light, talking more easily than they have ever done.

Marilla has seen them walking up the lane together from the kitchen window, and, to Anne's surprise, she does not seem displeased. She says quietly that she once quarrelled with Gilbert's father, John Blythe, when they were young, and that she was too proud to forgive him when he said he was sorry. It is a long time ago, she says, but she has often wished since then that she had been wiser.

In the autumn, Anne stands for the first time at the front of the Avonlea schoolroom, facing a row of curious young faces, some of which she remembers as little children. She is determined to be patient and kind, and to make every child in the room love learning as she has always loved it. Her heart is beating hard, but her voice is steady, and the lesson begins.

In the evenings, after the school day is done, Anne sits by the lamp and reads aloud to Marilla, who is resting her eyes as the doctor ordered. The headaches grow less, and when she goes again to Charlottetown, the specialist tells her that her sight is no worse, and may even be a little better. Marilla says that it is all thanks to Anne, and Anne says that it is all thanks to Marilla.

Anne and Diana remain the dearest of friends, and on fine afternoons they walk arm in arm along the roads where they once played as little girls. They talk of everything that lies before them, such as their work, their families and the places they hope to see, and they promise each other that nothing will ever change. Both of them know, deep down, that a great deal will change, and that this knowledge only makes the promise sweeter.

As the weeks go by, Anne discovers that she loves teaching, and that she is more patient than she had expected. She remembers exactly how it felt to be a small, odd child whom nobody understood, and she is very gentle with the pupils who find it hardest to learn. When a shy little girl at last gets a sum right, the delight on her face is worth more to Anne than any medal.

One evening Anne walks to the churchyard and kneels beside Matthew's grave, where the white roses that he loved are blooming in the dusk. She tells him quietly that she is trying to be a good daughter to Marilla and a good teacher to the children, and that she hopes he can see how things have turned out. The silence that answers her is warm and gentle, and she feels that he is near.

Anne walks home from the churchyard through the golden light of the evening, thinking about her life and how much it has changed. She remembers the thin, wild little girl who arrived on the train with a carpet bag and a head full of dreams, and she knows how much she has been given since then. The road is quiet, the orchards are dark against the sky, and a star appears over the hill.

Anne stops at the place where the road makes a sharp bend, and for a moment she cannot see what lies beyond it. Her old plans have changed, and her path is not the one she once imagined, but she is not afraid, because she believes that every turning holds its own beauty. With a glad heart she goes on toward the lamp that is waiting in the window of Green Gables, sure that the best is yet to come.
